stories.headline: Fantasy buzz: A.J. Brown, Sam Darnold injured in season opener
stories.summary: A.J. Brown and Sam Darnold could both miss time with injuries suffered in Wednesday's opener.
stories.body:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values in fantasy football.

Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

Sept. 10: A.J. Brown, Sam Darnold injured in season opener

Injuries were unfortunately the story of the first game of the season as both Sam Darnold (hip) and A.J. Brown (ankle) exited early. Both teams have a mini-bye now -- 11 days between games -- allowing extra time to potentially return, but their statuses need to be monitored. Adam Schefter reported that Darnold had a CT scan and the initial test was "encouraging but inconclusive." A fracture has been ruled out, per Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald.

If Darnold misses time, Drew Lock is the next man up, but he is an option only in superflex leagues. Jaxon Smith-Njigba showed he was QB-proof, finishing with 11 targets, eight catches, 122 yards, one touchdown and 26.2 fantasy points. Perhaps there is more weekly variance if Darnold remains out, but JSN remains a must-start WR1.

If Brown, who was seen leaving in a walking boot, were to miss time, DeMario Douglas and Romeo Doubs would be waiver wire options. Doubs would likely run most of the Brown routes, with Mack Hollins also mixing in. Douglas was the Patriots' top target in Week 1, but he finished with just 20 yards on five catches. There is more upside with Doubs, but both would be more depth pieces for fantasy purposes.

Other notable fantasy takeaways

Drake Maye had a rough night at the office, throwing three interceptions and finishing with just 9.82 fantasy points. The Seahawks' defense remains his kryptonite. Still, this is one of the very best defenses in the NFL, so fantasy managers should not overreact. Maye remains a must-start QB with a bounce-back opportunity against the Steelers in Week 2.
Jadarian Price was the lead back for Seattle, playing 50% of the snaps, with 10 carries and two targets. George Holani saw a lot of the early passing downs and the initial red zone snaps. It was Price's first NFL game, so do not overreact: he was used more late in the game, which shows the coaches' confidence in him. His usage should expand as the season goes on. However, he is a RB3/flex option until that happens. Especially considering there will be fewer scoring opportunities if Darnold is sidelined.
Rhamondre Stevenson saw elite usage with TreVeyon Henderson sidelined. He played 85% of the snaps with 18 of 24 RB carries. He also led the Patriots in routes and was second in targets. He finished with 95 total yards and 14.5 fantasy points. He is a must-start option if Henderson misses more time. If and when he returns, Stevenson will be a safe-floor RB2 or flex play, while Henderson is a high-upside flex option to start his season.
The Seahawks' defense created pressure 13 times, while picking up three sacks and three interceptions. They limited Stevenson to just 2.8 yards per carry. In total, they finished with 14 fantasy points and for now are a "set it and forget it" fantasy D/ST. Outside of your star players, you should do your best to avoid starting players against them.

Sept. 9: Bowers injury puts Mayer on the fantasy radar

By Eric Moody

Brock Bowers will miss the start of the 2026 season after undergoing a meniscus trim Tuesday. According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, the Raiders tight end is expected to miss "a game or two" after getting banged up during training camp.

That's a significant loss for a Las Vegas passing game already short on proven playmakers, and it gives veteran tight end Michael Mayer a much bigger role to start the season. The Raiders kick off the season at home vs. the Miami Dolphins before hitting the road in Week 2 to face the Los Angeles Chargers.

Mayer hasn't offered much fantasy value when Bowers has been on the field. In nine games with Bowers last season, he averaged just 2.9 targets and 3.4 fantasy points per game. His role changed considerably when Bowers was out, with Mayer averaging 6.0 targets and 10.9 fantasy points per game across four games. That makes Mayer an excellent streaming option while Bowers is sidelined.

Kirk Cousins also helps Mayer's outlook. Cousins has a long history of getting his tight ends involved in the passing game. He heavily targeted Jordan Reed (220 targets) in Washington from 2015 to 2016 and later leaned on Kyle Rudolph and T.J. Hockenson in Minnesota before working with Kyle Pitts Sr. in Atlanta.

Mayer obviously isn't Bowers, but there will be targets available while the starter is sidelined. Mayer has already shown that his usage can increase significantly in those situations. Tre Tucker should also benefit. He's projected to be the Raiders' No. 1 wide receiver and has finished in the top 10 at the position in both snaps and routes in each of the past two seasons.

Bowers remains an elite fantasy option when healthy. He caught 112 passes for 1,194 yards and five touchdowns as a rookie in 2024 before injuries affected his second season. This isn't expected to be a long-term absence. Until Bowers returns, Mayer is on the outside of the top 10 tight ends but is worth streaming consideration.

Sep. 9 News or noise: Love not listed as Cards' RB1

Adam Schefter reported Tuesday night that Tyler Allgeier has been listed as the Arizona Cardinals' RB1 with Jeremiyah Love their RB2, a move that only demands that we, as fantasy managers, now closely monitor Love's injury reports heading into Sunday's game. Depth chart listings often come with a good degree of coaching misdirection, such as the Washington Commanders listing rookie Jacory Croskey-Merritt as their RB4 entering Week 1 of last season, only to have him total as many rushing attempts (10) as the three men ahead of him on the depth chart as well as 14.2 fantasy points. I'm not dramatically dropping Love in my rankings yet, but the announcement is a reason to prefer Stevenson this week.

Sept. 7: What Tua being named starter means for Falcons

By Matt Bowen

With the Atlanta Falcons naming Tua Tagovailoa as the starting quarterback for the Week 1 game versus the Pittsburgh Steelers, let's discuss the fantasy implications for head coach Kevin Stefanski's offense.

From a scheme perspective, Tagovailoa is a fit for what Stefanski wants at the position. A timing and rhythm thrower, Tagovailoa can be set up to throw with accuracy (68% career completion percentage) in a heavy play-action pass game. Look for deep in-breakers to Drake London here, along with the crossers and intermediate throws to tight end Kyle Pitts Sr. Plus, I do see Stefanski scripting isolation targets for both London and Pitts to generate positive matchups for Tagovailoa.

As it stands, Tagovailoa has some value in deeper 2QB Superflex formats. London will stay as a lower-tier WR1 in my ranks, while Pitts remains a midtier TE1 -- with breakout game ability.

In the Falcons' backfield, there is no change with Bijan Robinson. Stefanski's offense will cater to Robinson's dual-threat ability with high-end rushing volume and receiving opportunities. You can lock him as an elite RB1.

Sept. 4: Names to know in deep/keeper leagues before your final drafts

By Michael F. Florio

Drafting this weekend in a deep or a keeper league and need some names to keep in mind? In deep leagues, you are looking for stashes that have the chance to return value later in the season. In keeper leagues, you are looking for the same, but more so with players that could be values in drafts next year as well. Here are players that you should not forget about if you're in these types of leagues.

WR Jordyn Tyson was a middle-round pick before his hamstring injury. The New Orleans Saints first-round pick is extremely talented, with a playcaller in Kellen Moore who has run a pass-first offense in the past. He is a fantastic IR stash who could blossom into a second-half contributor. Those in keeper leagues should draft and stash, as he is sure to be more expensive next season.
Seattle Seahawks RB Zach Charbonnet is eligible to return in Week 5. He likely returns to RB3 value shortly thereafter and can be found in the late rounds.
Las Vegas Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza is not starting to open the season, meaning he is likely going to be undrafted in many formats. Still, the No. 1 pick is tied to a strong play caller and two elite offensive players (Brock Bowers, Ashton Jeanty) around him. He will play at some point and, if he hits, he will shoot up draft boards next season. Those are the kind of chances worth taking in the later rounds of keeper leagues.
Miami Dolphins QB Malik Willis can be found in the later rounds of drafts and brings QB1 upside. Here is the stat to know: Since 2000, 44 QBs have ran 100-plus times in a season, with 60% of them averaging 20 fantasy PPG. All but five averaged 17.4 points per game, which was the criteria to be a QB1 in fantasy last season.
WRs Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell are potentially the top targets for Willis in Miami this year. Douglas has received rave reviews from Dolphins camp and played every snap in preseason with Willis. Bell had first-round NFL Draft hype before he tore his ACL. Both have the upside to become weekly contributors.
Jacksonville Jaguars WR/CB Travis Hunter is simply a bet on talent. We are unsure what his role/usage will look like and, due to that, he can be had in the late rounds of drafts. He has the capability to be a weekly fantasy contributor if the offensive role is big enough. Plus, think of the hype in a keeper league if he hits!
Baltimore Ravens WR Ja'Kobi Lane has a chance to become the WR2 this season. His red zone capabilities on an offense led by Lamar Jackson means he has the potential to "touchdown his way" to fantasy relevance, even as the WR3. With a strong rookie showing, Lane could climb into the middle rounds of drafts next year, making him worth a late-round flier in keeper leagues.
San Francisco 49ers RB Kaelon Black played over Jordan James in the preseason and seems like the RB2 for the Niners. We have seen many backup backs become fantasy relevant under Kyle Shanahan. He has RB2 upside if Christian McCaffrey were to miss time.
Tennessee Titans RB Nicholas Singleton is more for those in keeper leagues. He likely will not contribute early, but we could see him take over as the season goes on. The key here is that both Titans RBs (Tony Pollard, Tyjae Spears) are free agents after the season.

Sept. 1: Lions' Pacheco heads to IR, out four games

By Tristan H. Cockcroft

Signed in March to a one-year, $1.81 million deal to replace David Montgomery as Jahmyr Gibbs' backfield partner/primary backup, Isiah Pacheco on Tuesday was placed on injured reserve by the Detroit Lions, ruling him out for the season's first four games. Pacheco had been dealing with an MCL sprain, but coach Dan Campbell raised more recent concerns about the 27-year-old's back, which ultimately led to the IR decision.

Pacheco's absence thrusts Gibbs, already a fantasy football superstar and the No. 1 player being picked on average in ESPN leagues, further into the spotlight. Already an explosive runner -- he's nicknamed "Sonic" for a reason -- Gibbs is also one of the game's best receiving running backs as well as a sound goal-line runner who has converted 11 of his 15 career chances into scores. There's little to quibble about with his game, and with his backup situation no longer completely clear, he could be in for the kind of workload that produces historic stat totals.

Though I have had Bijan Robinson ranked ahead of Gibbs all preseason, I've swapped them following this news. Gibbs now has a clear edge at the position.

As for that backup situation, zero-RB drafters can add a new name to their list of late-round candidates: Jacob Saylors. The former UFL standout averaged 6.0 yards per carry this preseason and took four of his 31 rushing attempts for 10-plus yards. Fantasy managers in ESPN standard leagues can monitor Saylors' usage in Week 1, as the Lions had previously leaned heavily upon Montgomery, but Saylors is beneath the roster-worthy threshold unless his workload is within range of that.

stories.headline: Team USA scores 108 in rout of Hungary to reach FIBA semis
stories.summary: The U.S. routed Hungary 108-56 to advance to the semifinals of the women's FIBA World Cup and stretched its winning streak in the tournament to 34 games.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- Napheesa Collier scored 19 points as the U.S. routed Hungary 108-56 to advance to the semifinals of the women's FIBA World Cup on Thursday.

The U.S. will play the winner of the Spain-Australia game Saturday in the medal round. France played China and Belgium faced host Germany in the other quarterfinal matchups.

It was a record-breaking performance for the U.S., its 108 points the most by any team in a World Cup quarterfinal. The U.S. had 31 assists, again the most in this round.

"When that ball is moving, we want to get the best possible shot," said Kahleah Copper, who had 10 points. "We want to make sure everybody gets involved. Everyone here on this roster, we know what they're doing on their respective [WNBA] teams. But you come here, you sacrifice a little bit of that."

Copper said the players were always looking to turn good scoring opportunities into great ones. The Americans did just that.

The U.S. was off and running early against Hungary, jumping out to a 36-12 lead after the first quarter. The Americans were constantly pounding the ball inside and converting turnovers into easy layups. Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese showed their growing chemistry on the court, finishing the quarter with a nifty pick and roll just before the buzzer. Collier had 10 points in the first 10 minutes.

The offense was sizzling as the Americans hit 20 of their first 26 shots (76.9%), including 5 of 6 3-point attempts, to race to a 50-18 lead with six minutes left in the first half. The Americans led 59-30 at the break -- the highest scoring first half ever in the quarterfinals, according to FIBA.

The Americans got a little scare when Sonia Citron had to leave in the third quarter when she was hit in the nose by a Hungary player's hand by accident. Citron returned to start the fourth quarter.

Clark finished with 10 points and nine assists, just missing out on her second double-double of the tournament.

The U.S. was also solid on defense. It contained Hungary's top scorer, Dorka Juhasz, who plays for the Minnesota Lynx. She came into the game averaging 15.3 points and 11 rebounds in the tournament. She missed her first seven shots and didn't get her first basket until 2:26 was left in the half. She finished the game with two points on 1-for-12 shooting.

Hungary came away with its best World Cup finish by reaching the quarterfinals for the first time. Hungary was fifth in the 1957 tournament, but back then it was a round robin with no medal rounds.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey breakout forwards: Why Quinn, Coronato should take the next step
stories.summary: Sean breaks down which fantasy hockey forwards have the right conditions to break out this season.
stories.body:
Every fantasy draft turns on a breakout or two -- the player you reach for a round early because you're convinced this is the year it finally clicks. Hit on one and you've got a star at a role-player price. The catch is that "convinced" usually comes down to a hot preseason, a shiny new linemate, or a highlight that lodged in your brain in April.

So instead of guessing who looks ready, I went the other way. I pulled every forward who has actually broken out since 2009-10 and asked what they had in common at the moment it happened, what was true when the breakout happened.

Two things carry more signal than you'd expect: how old a player was, and how many NHL games he already had under him. Break out much younger and you're just betting on talent; much older and you're chasing an outlier that barely happens. There's a window, and it's narrower than the eye test would ever guess.

Here's the quick version of what I'm calling "ready":

The median fantasy points per game (FPPG) across the 1,700 individual top-100 forward seasons since 2009-10 is 1.90, and that's the bar we set for a breakout.

Using all game logs since the 2009-10 season, there are 299 forwards that have made more than one appearance among the top 100 for fantasy scoring. This purposefully excludes any one-time flukes.

Of those 299 forwards, 177 made their debut in 2009-10 or later, meaning we have complete game logs for their entire career.

Of those 177 forwards, 124 eventually held a rolling 41-game FPPG average above 1.90 for at least 41 consecutive games -- a half-season at that pace at minimum, and often longer.

The average age those 124 forwards had reached when that breakout run began was 24 years, 74 days (with the majority doing it between 21 years, 303 days and 26 years, 88 days).

The average experience those 124 forwards had when that run began was 250 games played (with the majority doing it between 142 and 399).

So those are the coordinates. What follows are the forwards sitting inside that window right now who haven't gotten there yet -- because a player who's already banked a top-100 season isn't a breakout, he's a known quantity. These are the ones the math says are due.

More: Sign up for free | Rankings | Projections | League types

The breakouts

Ridly Greig, C, Ottawa Senators (24.1 years old, 1.24 FPPG in 247 games played): Admittedly, Greig isn't my first choice from the list of qualified players, but he's listed first because he is almost exactly the breakout age and experience. He's also going to find himself with a regular top-six role based on the Sens' current depth chart.

Jack Quinn, RW, Buffalo Sabres (25.0 years old, 1.27 FPPG in 260 games played): There are a few different configurations that could play out for the Sabres' scoring lines, but Quinn is firmly in the mix to be a part of them on the wings. There is even a conceivable path here that lands him with top power-play time if he can take the next step.

Matt Coronato, RW, Calgary Flames (23.8 years old, 1.28 FPPG in 192 games played): Has a door been this wide open for young prospects to take the leap before? The Flames' teardown has left them with no choice but to thrust players like Coronato into the limelight. Just watch out for that plus-minus if your custom league still uses it.

Bobby Brink, RW, Minnesota Wild (25.2 years old, 1.15 FPPG in 214 games played): Brink was on his way to a 20-goal season with the Flyers in limited ice time, before the trade to the Wild further cut into his opportunities. Now, Minnesota has some flexibility for new faces to earn key roles and Brink will be in the mix.

Logan Stankoven, C, Carolina Hurricanes (23.5 years old, 1.27 FPPG in 183 games played): The Stanley Cup playoffs were a coming out party for Stankoven, who could have earned himself a Conn Smythe Trophy if Jordan Staal's goals weren't more timely. His line with Jackson Blake and Taylor Hall should hit the ground running in the regular season.

Egor Chinakhov, RW, Pittsburgh Penguins (25.6 years old, 1.19 FPPG in 247 games played): Remember the key breakout threshold we set was high, at 1.90 FPPG. Well, Chinkhov had 1.88 FPPG over the final 43 games of the season after the trade to the Penguins. He essentially already broke out, even if the math didn't quite catch it on a technicality.

Mackie Samoskevich, LW, Seattle Kraken (23.8 years old, 1.23 FPPG in 156 games played): Seattle spent a first-round pick to spring him from Florida's forward logjam, specifically to turn loose his shooter's mentality on a scoring line, likely alongside Shane Wright. He lived among the league leaders in shots per 60 (64th among forwards with at least 100 minutes) on limited Panthers ice time; give him the minutes and the counting stats follow.

Mavrik Bourque, C, Nashville Predators (24.6 years old, 1.06 FPPG in 156 games played): Nashville gave him $33 million and a projected second-line center job -- a massive linemate upgrade for a guy who broke out for 20 goals buried in Dallas' bottom six.

Connor McMichael, C, St. Louis Blues (25.6 years old, 1.21 FPPG in 315 games played): The Jordan Kyrou trade sent him to St. Louis, and his 26-goal, 57-point 2024-25 is the reminder of his top-six ceiling. Just note the Blues also added Mason McTavish down the middle, so McMichael may shuffle between center and wing. The minutes stay top-six, the exact role won't.

Emil Heineman, LW, New York Islanders (24.8 years old, 1.29 FPPG in 148 games played): Riding Bo Horvat's wing, Heineman busted out for 22 goals against just nine assists -- a lopsided line that pegs him as a finisher, not a facilitator. If he holds that top-line spot the goals are real, but treat him as a goals-and-hits multi-category piece and keep the points expectations in check.

Jackson Blake, RW, Carolina Hurricanes (23.1 years old, 1.25 FPPG in 162 games played): Blake closed the playoffs on Carolina's most dangerous line, flanking Stankoven and Hall for a plus-30 across 19 games. That trio should open the year intact on a Cup contender, making the 23-year-old a cheap ticket into one of the league's better even-strength units.

Shane Wright, C, Seattle Kraken (22.7 years old, 1.31 FPPG in 169 games played): We've been penciling in a Wright breakout since draft night, and the pedigree has cashed exactly zero of those checks so far. The difference this time isn't the talent, it's that he's finally banked enough NHL games to be sitting right in the breakout window, with a top-six role that's his to lose.

Marco Kasper, C, Detroit Red Wings (22.4 years old, 1.25 FPPG in 159 games played): Kasper's sophomore crash to nine goals on a 6.9 shooting percentage screams undervalued, especially now that he's healthy after gutting through a knee injury. The swing factor is Dylan Larkin, as a trade vaults Kasper into a top-six role where the shooting luck corrects. If Larkin stays, he's more of a late-round dart.

Frank Nazar, C, Chicago Blackhawks (22.6 years old, 1.43 FPPG in 122 games played): With Connor Bedard shelved into November following shoulder surgery, Nazar will be leaned on in the early season. He buried only 15 of 138 shots last season, so positive regression is coming, and the Bedard-less minutes are his runway to cash in before the role tightens up.

Test out your strategies with the ESPN Mock Draft Lobby.

You again?

A few players were highlighted for this same list last season, but are still in the wheelhouse for a breakout. It's never too late.

Luke Evangelista, RW, New Jersey Devils (24.5 years old, 1.18 FPPG in 253 games played): Surprising late offseason trade to the Devils aside, Evangelista was making this list regardless. He has the skills and budding experience to break through as a fantasy-relevant winger. He's a lock for an opportunity alongside either Nico Hischier or Jack Hughes, which is arguably more enticing than the same top-six chances in Nashville.

Kent Johnson, LW, Columbus Blue Jackets (23.9 years old, 1.14 FPPG in 274 games played): Johnson already flashed the ceiling -- 57 points in 2024-25 -- before a shoulder injury and a career-worst 6.1 shooting percentage buried the followup. But a breakout absolutely requires him to beat out Valeri Nichushkin and/or Conor Garland for the top power-play unit.

Cole Perfetti, LW, Winnipeg Jets (24.7 years old, 1.28 FPPG in 290 games played): We keep waiting on the power-play leap, and Perfetti keeps getting stranded on the wrong unit, with just six power-play points last season despite career-high man-advantage minutes. He's shown 50-point ability, so if Winnipeg finally hands him a true PP1 look behind Kyle Connor and Mark Scheifele, the breakout follows; until then he's a late-round bet on that door opening.

Tyson Foerster, RW, Philadelphia Flyers (24.6 years old, 1.54 FPPG in 195 games played): Foerster carries the highest floor in this tier, thanks to an elite shot and a top-six role with Trevor Zegras plus PP1 time. A November surgery wiped out most of his 2025-26, but he'd banked 13 goals in 29 games before it, and with a healthy runway for once, the 30-goal season people keep projecting becomes the base case.

Mason McTavish, C, St. Louis Blues (23.6 years old, 1.46 FPPG in 304 games played): The former No. 3 pick finally gets a change of scenery in St. Louis, where a projected second-line center job behind Robert Thomas could unlock the offense that stalled in Anaheim. His 2025-26 (41 points in 75 games) underwhelmed, but he's only 23 with real pedigree.

stories.headline: NBA offseason recap, early 2026-27 season previews by team
stories.summary: We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the regular season by rolling out one team profile each weekday through Sept. 18.
stories.body:
After an eventful July full of big trades, intriguing signings and the game's biggest star shocking everyone by heading East, the NBA offseason is nearly complete. And with the regular-season schedule now out, it's time to start thinking about the 2026-27 season.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for every team.

Check out the rollout schedule below, with stories added daily:

Quick links:

Free agency buzz | FA grades | Trade grades

Transactions | Schedule | More NBA coverage

Central Division

Milwaukee Bucks: Sept. 7
Key additions: Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, Caris LeVert

Key retentions: Gary Trent Jr.

Key subtractions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bobby Portis

After 13 seasons, the Giannis era ended in Milwaukee with a mega trade to the Heat -- and the 2026-27 season will mark a major shift for the rebuilding franchise.

The Bucks hired coach Taylor Jenkins to establish a culture. They added four new players from Miami, including former All-Star and Wisconsin native Tyler Herro, and selected Brayden Burries with the No. 10 pick in June.

The Bucks will enter the season with an ill-fitting mix of players and low expectations, but they have the luxury to see what sticks long term. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bucks offseason recap/season preview

Chicago Bulls: Sept. 8
Key additions: F Caleb Wilson, G Dailyn Swain, C Nic Claxton, G Norman Powell, Tiago Splitter

Key subtractions: None

Key retentions: F Zach Collins

For years, Chicago has been seen as one of the sleeping giants of the NBA, a once-proud franchise reduced to meandering in the play-in tournament and in the middle of the lottery in recent seasons. But the Bulls got a much-needed makeover this summer and enter the 2026-27 season with a clearer direction than they've had in years.

The changes have been full-scale: Bryson Graham was hired as the team's new head of basketball operations, Tiago Splitter will patrol the sidelines as head coach, No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson is the new face of the franchise, and he'll be surrounded by some veterans like Nic Claxton and Norman Powell to help ease his transition. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bulls offseason recap/season preview

Cleveland Cavaliers: Sept. 9
Key additions: Peyton Watson, Mario Hezonja

Key subtractions: Dean Wade, Dennis Schroder, Max Strus, Larry Nance Jr., Caris Levert, Keon Ellis

Key retentions: Donovan Mitchell, James Harden

The Cavs' failed pursuit of LeBron James this summer turned into a pivot for a younger, athletic wing, prying Watson from the Nuggets after a career-year.

Watson averaged career highs in points, rebounds, assists and steals while shooting 41% from 3 last year, and he has in recent years been one of the strongest wing defenders in the league. That makes him a strong complement next to James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, as the Cavs hope he can provide a substantial answer to the elusive fifth starter role next to their core four. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Cavaliers offseason recap/season preview

Detroit Pistons: Sept. 10
Key additions: John Collins, Isaiah Joe, Taurean Prince, Gary Harris

Key subtractions: Tobias Harris, Isaiah Stewart

Key retentions: None

The Pistons' offseason is still in limbo as negotiations with restricted free agent Jalen Duren have stalled.

Detroit believes it sent Duren a fair offer considering the totality of his 2025-26 season -- including his underwhelming playoff showing -- while Duren feels like he's checked off all the boxes to get more.

Losing Harris and Stewart will be a big test to their culture -- or a signal they have to win a different way than in the last two seasons.

They added shooting on the margins with Joe, Prince and Harris. And assuming Duren's deal gets done before camp, Ausar Thompson's contract is next on the docket. -- Vincent Goodwill

Read the full Pistons offseason recap/season preview

Indiana Pacers: Sept. 11

Southeast Division

Miami Heat: Aug. 31
Key additions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson, Bobby Portis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Nick Richards

Key retentions: Andrew Wiggins, Simone Fontecchio

Key subtractions: Tyler Herro, Norman Powell, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis

Heat president Pat Riley landed the superstar he'd been searching for since LeBron James left Miami in 2016. Antetokounmpo is in the fold, and Miami is ready to contend for another title with the two-time MVP. Antetokounmpo is just as motivated to win his second title and remind everyone that he can be the best player in the league.

In the trade, the Heat gave up key players such as Herro, Ware and Jaquez and did not bring back Powell in free agency. They landed Thompson to a two-year, $13 million deal after the four-time champion sharpshooter worked out a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Miami also added Portis and Hardaway, but the team is still looking to bolster the roster around Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Heat offseason recap/season preview

Washington Wizards: Sept. 1
Key additions: AJ Dybantsa, Khris Middleton, Deandre Ayton, Tre Mann

Key subtractions: Cam Whitmore, D'Angelo Russell, Jaden Hardy

Key retentions: Trae Young

The Wizards got their jump on this pivotal offseason by acquiring Trae Young and Anthony Davis last season in trades.

Those were their two big moves and then came the big prize for losing 65 games last season - winning the lottery and drafting AJ Dybantsa with the first overall pick.

Ready to start winning games this season after losing 60 or more games in each of the past three years, Washington gave Young a four-year, $212 million contract. The Wizards added veterans like Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton to bolster the depth behind their young core featuring the likes of Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, Tre Johnson and Will Riley. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Wizards offseason recap/season preview

Charlotte Hornets: Sept. 2
Key additions: F Naz Reid, G Grayson Allen, G Dennis Schroder, F Royce O'Neale, F Dorian Finney-Smith

Key retentions: G Coby White

Key subtractions: G LaMelo Ball, F Miles Bridges, G Josh Green, G Tre Mann

After enjoying their best season in a decade, the Hornets sharply changed course with the surprising decision to trade Ball, their franchise guard, to the Timberwolves.

Given that Ball was a borderline All-Star on a max contract, Charlotte opted for a "Moneyball" approach in hopes of avoiding the perpetual mediocrity that tripped up Trae Young's Atlanta Hawks in the recent past.

With Ball and starting forward Miles Bridges moved in separate deals aimed at collecting future draft assets and improving its cap flexibility, Charlotte is now the only team that doesn't have a single player on the books for at least $25 million next season. -- Ben Golliver

Atlanta Hawks: Sept. 3
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason.

The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall.

Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Orlando Magic: Sept. 4
Key additions: C Nikola Vucevic, G Izaiyah Nelson

Key subtractions: F Moritz Wagner, G Jett Howard

Key retentions: F Jonathan Isaac, G Jevon Carter

The Magic's biggest move this offseason was hiring Sean Sweeney to replace Jamahl Mosley.

Orlando also brought Nikola Vucevic back on a one-year, $3.9 million deal since trading him in 2021 and will use his ability to score and shoot to space the floor for Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Desmond Bane.

The Magic blew a 3-1 lead over top-seeded Detroit in the first round of the playoffs after Wagner went down due to injury and were in desperate need of someone who can get easier baskets and make outside shots. Vucevic should help. Moe Wagner departed for Brooklyn via free agency, separating Franz from his brother for the first time in his pro career. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Magic offseason recap/season preview

Pacific Division

Los Angeles Lakers: Aug. 24
Key additions: C Walker Kessler, F Sandro Mamukelashvili, G Quentin Grimes, G Collin Sexton, F Kevon Looney, F Matisse Thybulle, G Cameron Carr

Key retentions: G Austin Reaves

Key subtractions: F LeBron James, C Deandre Ayton, G Marcus Smart, F Rui Hachimura, G Luke Kennard, C Jaxson Hayes

James informed the Lakers he would not be returning for next season on June 30. Two days later, the team transformed the roster, with Doncic squarely as the focal point.

The biggest addition -- literally and figuratively -- is 7-foot-2 center Kessler, acquired in a sign-and-trade deal with the Utah Jazz. L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and pick swaps in 2028 and 2030, not to mention a four-year, $130 million contract, to acquire him.

Mamukelashvili, Grimes, Sexton, Looney and Thybulle also signed with the Lakers, and free agent Ziaire Williams and first-round pick Carr bolster the team's young prospect pool of Adou Thiero, Bronny James and Dalton Knecht.

The most important move, though, came when Reaves, coming off a career season in which he averaged 23.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game, signed a four-year, $180 million extension.

When the dust settled, it was a dramatic roster overhaul in what could prove to be one of the most consequential summers in franchise history, with the team also being sold for the second time in 14 months, this time to venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, who bought the Lakers from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Lakers offseason recap/season preview

LA Clippers: Aug. 25
Key additions: Rui Hachimura, Keaton Wagler, Brandon Ingram (TBD), Gradey Dick (TBD)

Key retentions: Kobe Sanders, Bradley Beal

Key subtractions: Kawhi Leonard (TBD), Nicolas Batum, Bogdan Bogdanovic, John Collins

What started as a reconfiguration at the trade deadline -- acquiring Darius Garland from Cleveland for James Harden and Bennedict Mathurin from Indiana for Ivica Zubac -- turned into a complete overhaul this summer after the Clippers let Bogdan Bogdanovic, Nicolas Batum and John Collins walk.

Their biggest move, however, was trading Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks, but that deal is in limbo pending the investigation into alleged salary cap circumvention by the team relating to Leonard's Aspiration endorsement deal.

In the meantime, LA added Illinois guard Wagler with the No. 5 pick in the draft and signed Hachimura away from the crosstown Lakers with a two-year, $28 million deal. And in a surprise move, Bradley Beal -- after declining his $5.6 million contract option for next season in June to test free agency -- ended up re-signing on a two-year, $13.2 million deal in mid-August to stay with the Clippers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Clippers offseason recap/season preview

Golden State Warriors: Aug. 26
Key additions: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Georges Niang

Key subtractions: Quinten Post, Pat Spencer

Key retentions: Draymond Green, Al Horford, Kristaps Porzingis, Gary Payton II, De'Anthony Melton

The Warriors opted for flexibility and stability over a larger shake-up around Curry. Their much-publicized recruitment of James never gained much traction.

They brought back their veteran frontcourt trio (Green, Horford, Porzingis), but kept them all on short-term maneuverable contracts. They opted for the fit of Melton over a pursuit of scoring guard Anfernee Simons. Their big addition is Lendeborg, the 23-year-old rookie wing who they will rely upon to be a high-minute, high-impact rotation player immediately.

In the bigger picture, they protected their draft pick cupboard and lined up their books to have an ocean of cap space as they peer a bit deeper into the future while their core ages. -- Anthony Slater

Phoenix Suns: Aug. 27
Key additions: F Miles Bridges, F Koa Peat, G Luke Kennard

Key subtractions: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale

Key retentions: F Dillon Brooks, G Collin Gillespie, C Mark Williams, G Jordan Goodwin

Phoenix followed up its surprising season with a series of moves to mostly keep its team intact, with some adjustments around the margins.

The Suns re-signed Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Williams (three years, $38 million), Goodwin (three years, $19 million) and Brooks (three years, $73 million) to new deals and made a major splash by trading Allen and O'Neale to the Charlotte Hornets for Bridges. And despite not having a pick until No. 47 in the second round of the 2026 draft, Phoenix was able to acquire Arizona player Peat -- who averaged 14.1 points on 52.8% shooting as a freshman for the Wildcats and was key to their Final Four run. -- Dave McMenamin

Sacramento Kings: Aug. 28
Key additions: G Darius Acuff Jr., F Alex Karaban, G Emanuel Sharp

Key subtractions: G DeMar DeRozan, G Russell Westbrook

Key retentions: F Precious Achiuwa

Perry, currently in the organization's power seat, is continuing a steady transition toward the younger core he has drafted. Arkansas guard and No. 7 pick Acuff is the spotlight name on a roster populated with six players in their first two NBA seasons.

But they still have notable high-minute holdovers from the past regime, including Murray, Malik Monk, LaVine and Sabonis. Of those four, Murray appears the most locked-in as a stable member of the team's long-term vision. Perry explored trades for Monk, LaVine and Sabonis over the past year, but didn't value the proposed returns, and the three are expected to open the season in Sacramento. -- Anthony Slater

Northwest Division

Portland Trail Blazers: Aug. 17
Key additions: G Ja Morant, F Jeremy Sochan

Key retentions: C Robert Williams III

Key subtractions: F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, G Matisse Thybulle

Sadly, the Blazers made far more noise this offseason with their off-court business dealings than anything they did with their roster. New owner Tom Dundon's aggressive cost-cutting measures and ongoing fight for arena financing have distracted from the progress that Portland made on the court last season, when it reached the playoffs for the first time since 2021.

Although the Blazers were the only team that sat out June's draft by not making a pick, they will add two high-profile guards to a rotation that otherwise looks very similar to last season. Lillard, a franchise icon, is back from an Achilles tendon injury that sidelined him for the entire 2025-26 campaign, and Morant, a two-time All-Star, arrived in a trade that sent Grant and Murray to the Memphis Grizzlies. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Blazers offseason recap/season preview

Utah Jazz: Aug. 18
Key additions: G Darryn Peterson, C Jaxson Hayes, G Josh Okogie

Key retentions: C Jusuf Nurkic

Key subtractions: C Walker Kessler

The Jazz finally got some lottery luck, landing at No. 2 and taking Peterson, a gifted guard who has the potential to emerge as the face of the franchise. The hope was that Peterson would be the final major piece in Utah's rebuild, but that plan featured Kessler as the team's long-term starting center. Instead, the Jazz agreed to a sign-and-trade deal that sent Kessler to the Lakers in exchange for a pair of future first-round picks and two swaps.

The return was widely considered to be great value for Utah, particularly after Kessler's deal (four years, $130 million) pushed beyond the Jazz's comfort zone, but there is now a glaring need in the starting lineup alongside Jackson and Lauri Markkanen in the frontcourt. -- Tim MacMahon

Minnesota Timberwolves: Aug. 19
Key additions: G LaMelo Ball, G Josh Green, G Isaiah Evans

Key subtractions: F Julius Randle, C Naz Reid

Key retentions: G Ayo Dosunmu, G Bones Hyland, G Jaylen Clark

Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly continued to show his aggression, orchestrating a four-team trade with the Brooklyn Nets, Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets that sent out three-time All-Star Randle and the 2023-24 Sixth Man of the Year, Reid, and a future first-round pick to bring in the talented -- but polarizing -- Ball.

That move followed Connelly inking 6-foot-4 guard Dosunmu to a five-year, $112 million extension in June, following his acquisition at the deadline.

Minnesota also re-signed wing Clark and guard Hyland and acquired the 6-foot-6 Evans out of Duke with the No. 33 pick in the draft.

Coach Chris Finch also lost his top lieutenant on the bench, Micah Nori, who left to coach the Portland Trail Blazers. -- Dave McMenamin

Oklahoma City Thunder: Aug. 20
Key additions: C Aday Mara, G Bennett Stirtz

Key retentions: G Kenrich Williams, C Isaiah Hartenstein

Key subtractions: G Isaiah Joe, G Aaron Wiggins, G Luguentz Dort

The extensions for both Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren triggered in July, leading to a trio of financially motivated trades to slash the tax bill and cost-control the current roster.

They sent Isaiah Joe to Detroit and traded Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort to Atlanta in separate moves, eroding their depth.

General manager Sam Presti made clear in an interview with The Oklahoman that the impression he's been given from ownership is "the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

That would mean extra breathing room to eventually extend core young players such as Cason Wallace and Ajay Mitchell. Wallace, the likely replacement starter for Dort, is extension eligible off his rookie contract into October. -- Anthony Slater

Denver Nuggets: Aug. 21
Key additions: Marvin Bagley III, Lonnie Walker IV

Key retentions: Spencer Jones, Tyus Jones

Key subtractions: Watson, Tim Hardaway Jr., Jonas Valanciunas

Finding a resolution to Watson's restricted free agency was Denver's most important piece of summer business.

Watson is a draft success story, rising from the 30th overall pick into one of the league's more intriguing young two-way wings. But retaining the 23-year-old would have been expensive -- via either a sky-high luxury tax bill or a salary-slashing move to get off an important veteran and generate more breathing room for a new deal.

After Wednesday's deal to send Watson to Cleveland, Denver's front office can shift its attention to escaping the salary cap's second apron. The Nuggets are currently the league's only team above it. -- Anthony Slater

Key additions: F Cameron Boozer, G D'Angelo Russell, F Isaiah Stewart, F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, C Quinten Post

Key retentions: None

Key subtractions: G Ja Morant, F Santi Aldama

Memphis finally traded Ja Morant, turning the last page from an ultimately disappointing chapter in franchise history, and already has his replacement as the face of the franchise in place: No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer. GM Zach Kleiman has overhauled the roster in the past few transaction cycles, acquiring four first-round picks when he traded Desmond Bane, a few more when he dealt Jaren Jackson Jr. and none for Morant, whose departure signaled a fresh start for the Grizzlies and him.

Memphis is in a full-blown youth movement, as 21-year-old forward GG Jackson is now the longest-tenured player on the roster. The Grizzlies say they believe they have a long-term foundation in place with their last few lottery picks: center Zach Edey, small forward Cedric Coward and power forward Boozer. -- Tim MacMahon

Despite capturing a combined 47 wins over the last two seasons under executive vice president Joe Dumars and general manager Troy Weaver, the Pelicans clearly believe that internal growth is the best path forward. Perhaps that justifies a near-silent summer in which the hiring of new coach Jamahl Mosley turned out to be the team's most notable move. Mosley becomes New Orleans' third coach since Dumars took the helm in April 2025. In addition to drafting Jaron Pierre Jr. in the second round, New Orleans signed just two new players over the summer in Kobe Bufkin and Hunter Dickinson, while bringing back 14 of the 15 players from last season's squad. -- Michael C. Wright

The major changes made by the Mavericks this offseason were in the managerial and coaching ranks. After a seasonlong search, team governor Patrick Dumont hired Masai Ujiri to run the franchise's basketball operations, bringing the architect of the Toronto Raptors' 2019 title team to Dallas. Ujiri decided to part ways with coach Jason Kidd and recruited Dusty May, fresh off an NCAA title with Michigan, to replace him.

Johnson, who played for May at Michigan before the Mavs selected him with the No. 9 pick in the draft, is the headliner of the additions to the roster. Dallas added three potential immediate contributors in a six-team deal, acquiring former Grizzlies forward Santi Aldama, ex-Pistons guard Marcus Sasser and EuroLeague veteran Tarik Biberovic. The franchise also landed former No. 1 pick as part of the trade that sent Luguentz Dort from the Oklahoma City Thunder to the Atlanta Hawks. -- MacMahon

After suffering a first-round postseason exit for the second consecutive season, the Rockets resisted the temptation to jump into the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes after adding former MVP Durant last summer. General manager Rafael Stone and coach Ime Udoka will instead lean on growth from the team's collection of young talent acquired in recent years, not to mention the continuity that comes with those players developing together over multiple seasons.

Houston signed Tari Eason to a five-year, $81.5 million extension over the summer. But outside of that, the Rockets focused on bolstering depth by bringing aboard veterans Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic. The club also brought in renowned shooting coach Chip Engelland from Oklahoma City. Engelland spent more than a decade with the San Antonio Spurs, winning two titles. -- Wright

Wembanyama did it to keep San Antonio's talented young core together for as long as possible, with added flexibility to acquire needed supporting players. The Spurs grabbed one of those in free agency in Harris, an experienced, reliable scorer who adds size (6-foot-8, 226 pounds) and physicality on defense while bolstering frontcourt depth in the draft. -- Wright

stories.summary: Club Brugge striker Nicolo Tresoldi has emerged as a potential target for both Manchester United and Tottenham. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Club Brugge striker Nicolo Tresoldi has emerged as a potential target for both Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur could battle it out over the signing of Club Brugge striker Nicolo Tresoldi, according to TEAMtalk. The report states that both clubs recently scouted the 22-year-old, as he featured for the Belgian side against Aston Villa in the Champions League. Tresoldi scored a penalty in the match, though Club Brugge went on to lose 3-2, while his impact was felt last season with 23 goals. As both United and Spurs consider possible striker options, with doubts surrounding the future of Joshua Zirkzee and Richarlison respectively, Tresoldi could be caught in a transfer tug-of-war between the Premier League sides.

- Martín Zubimendi could push to leave Arsenal in January if the midfielder isn't featuring regularly for the side. TEAMtalk claims that the Spaniard is hoping to win back a place in the side, with Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly preferred at present by Mikel Arteta. Zubimendi only signed for Arsenal last summer, but uncertainty over his place in the team has led to links with Chelsea and Real Madrid. The report claims that both sides remain keen on the 27-year-old, should he become available.

- Newly-promoted LaLiga outfit Málaga have made an offer to sign Anthony Martial, reports transfer journalist Matteo Moretto. The striker is a free agent after leaving Mexican club Monterrey, and has been linked with several teams since the transfer window closed. The 30-year-old, who previously featured for Lyon, Monaco, and Manchester United, played 20 times for Monterrey, scoring once and assisting three times.

- Atlético Madrid star Álex Baena has been shortlisted as a potential future transfer target for Manchester City, according to Football Insider. The forward, who has a contract until 2030 with Atleti, has caught the eye of City boss Enzo Maresca, after an impressive year. However, Atleti are not planning on an exit, which could complicate a move.

- Chelsea are looking to reward Estêvão with a new and improved contract in the coming months. The Telegraph claims the club view the Brazil winger as "untouchable", despite a difficult start under Xabi Alonso. The manager has preferred a front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer, and Morgan Rogers, which has raised questions over the 19-year-old's future. However, Chelsea are keen to keep the youngster committed to the project after an impressive breakout campaign last time out, after he picked up eight goals and four assists in all competitions.

Other rumors
- Real Madrid are monitoring Declan Rice's future at Arsenal. The midfielder could become a priority target, while his contract runs until 2028. (Ekrem Konur)

- Premier League sides Arsenal and Manchester City are monitoring PSG defender Willian Pacho as a future transfer target. (Ekrem Konur)

- Kaoru Mitoma looks unlikely to sign a new contract extension with Brighton. The Japanese winger only has one year left on his deal, and could leave in January. (TeamTalk)

- Club America is looking at the possibility of signing former Bayern Munich and Real Madrid defender David Alaba as a free agent. (Matteo Moretto)

- Liverpool and Real Madrid remain interested in a potential future move for Bayern Munich and France star Michael Olise. (Christian Falk)

- Liverpool were considering challenging Chelsea for Marco Palestra in the summer. The Reds decided against a move for the right back, who was at Atalanta at the time, opting to improve elsewhere in the squad. (The Athletic)

- Manchester United are willing to offer a new long-term contract to Lisandro Martinez, if the defender can stay injury-free this season. The 27-year-old has one year left on his deal, though it includes an extra year option that can be triggered. (Football Insider)

- Links surrounding Everton and a move for free agents Anthony Martial and Mauro Icardi have been played down. The Toffees are looking at strikers for January, with a long-term fit in mind over a short-term fix. (The i Paper)
