stories.headline: Max Verstappen admits to McLaren, Mercedes talks before 'following heart' with Red Bull stay
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has admitted to serious talks with McLaren and Mercedes before agreeing his Red Bull extension last month.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen has admitted to serious talks with McLaren and Mercedes before agreeing his Red Bull extension last month.

Verstappen ended a long period of uncertainty about his future with the new Red Bull deal, announced ahead of his home race, the Dutch Grand Prix, which overwrote a deal lasting until 2028 with one running through to the end of 2030.

The existence of escape clauses in his old deal had allowed rumours of moves elsewhere to spread.

Verstappen has acknowledged that he explored options with rival teams before committing to a longer deal.

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously," Verstappen said in a BBC Sport interview when asked about how serious talks were with McLaren and Mercedes. "They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that."

Verstappen has been with Red Bull for his entire Formula 1 career. The company signed him to a developmental deal in 2014 before handing him a debut with junior team Toro Rosso the following season.

He memorably won for Red Bull on his first appearance with the team after replacing Daniil Kvyat at the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix.

He spent five seasons at the team before winning his first championship in 2021, the first of four consecutive titles.

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about the Madring

- Red Bull sign Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11

- Leclerc advice for Max vs. 100 drivers: Don't crash!

Verstappen pointed out he could have left Red Bull in those fallow years and ultimately opted to stay this time around as he believes Red Bull can be contenders again in future.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice," he said. "You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

Part of the uncertainty around Verstappen's future had been linked to his discontent with Formula 1's controversial new hybrid engines, which have shifted a lot of emphasis onto energy management and deployment.

Verstappen has labelled this "anti-racing" and likened the new F1 to Mario Kart.

F1 is making tweaks to the engines in 2027 and 2028 to lessen the importance of the electrical elements and Verstappen hopes this will lead to an improvement in how the racing feels.

"Hoping that it will be better in the future," he said. "Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

stories.headline: How Holbrook inspired Newcastle's remarkable turnaround
stories.summary: Newcastle have scored an extra 12.3 points per game in 2026 compared to last year's wooden-spoon season, making for the fourth greatest improvement in history.
stories.body:
It took just one meeting for Justin Holbrook to start providing the belief for the fourth greatest attacking turnaround in Australian rugby league history.

With Newcastle players arriving for day one of pre-season, Holbrook's first move was to make clear last year's wooden spoon was irrelevant.

"There was obviously a lot of outside noise," five-eighth Fletcher Sharpe recalled.

"But Justin sat us down and said: 'Look, I don't really care about what happened last year - it's a new year and looking at the squad in front of me, I know we can take it all out'."

Brought in after Adam O'Brien's Newcastle exit, Holbrook immediately made his mark.

"He said we had to come together and buy into a style. And we can win the comp," added halfback Sandon Smith, who had worked with Holbrook at the Sydney Roosters.

"We bought in from November 1.

"It wasn't a moment throughout the season where we thought, 'Oh wait we can actually do this'. It was built into us from the first day."

Ahead of Friday night's elimination final against South Sydney, Holbrook's Newcastle turnaround is statistically one of the greatest in history.

And at the centre of it all is Newcastle's attack, with players quick to heap praise on assistant Stephen Hales.

Newcastle were kept scoreless in 11 halves of football in 2025, and had the NRL's worst attack.

Such is the improvement, the Knights are scoring an extra 12.3 points per game this year.

Only three sides in the game's 118-year history have had a greater increase, with Parramatta in 2001 the last side to have such a dramatic rise.

While Newcastle scored five tries from the other side of halfway last year, this year they have the most in the NRL with 30.

And 63 tries have also originated from outside the attacking 20-metre zone, compared to 18 last season.

"It's a fun style to play," Sharpe said.

"I remember at the start it seemed expansive and off the cuff, but the whole team bought into it.

"It allows our strike players on the edges to get plenty of ball and do their thing.

"It's probably a style not everyone plays, so it gives a difference and plenty of variety too, which you need at this time of year."

Remarkably, Newcastle are having less play-the-balls on the opposition tryline and running similar metres per game to last year.

But they are far more efficient and have a willingness to shift more often from their own end, giving their fast and powerful outside backs early ball to play with.

Wingers Dom Young and Greg Marzhew have 62 linebreaks and 44 tries between them.

Kalyn Ponga remains at the heart of the attack, but hooker Phoenix Crossland believes the rise of Sharpe has taken some pressure off the Newcastle No.1.

"We're attacking nothing like we used to last year," Crossland said.

"That happens with new coaches and fresh ideas, with boys buying into our system."

Impressive too is the fact the rise has come with Newcastle rarely at full strength, with Sharpe, Ponga and the now-injured Dylan Brown having stints out.

"The strength of our coaching staff is just letting individuals express themselves," Ponga said.

"Every team's got systems, but what they've done a good job of is just giving you that belief that you can play your footy.

"That's just the way that they frame everything up, that there's no limit on what you can be."

GREATEST YEAR-ON-YEAR ATTACKING IMPROVEMENTS:

Balmain (1944): +16.0 points per game

Eastern Suburbs (1935): +14.4

Parramatta (2001): +14.0

Newcastle (2026): +12.3

Manly (2021): 12.2

stories.headline: Commanders' crab stuffed pretzel headlines new NFL 2026 foods
stories.summary: The latest NFL season has no shortage of unique concession items that will debut across stadiums.
stories.body:
When it comes to the NFL, the league seems to level up each season. The same applies to foods debuting at league stadiums.

Arguably the best from any team is a crab stuffed pretzel sold at Northwest Stadium, home of the Washington Commanders. The crab-shaped pretzel is filled with lemon tarragon crab dip topped with garlic butter and grated parmesan cheese created by Levy Restaurants.

Here's a look at some of the top new foods at NFL stadiums this season.

Pittsburgh Steelers: Black N' Gold Chicken and Waffle

The iconic colors of the Steelers are represented in a classic Southern meal that includes fried chicken, coleslaw, bacon jam, sweet potato fries and hot honey.

Philadelphia Eagles: Tush Push Taters

Philadelphia fans have seen their share of success with the tush push in recent years. Now, the play has a meal named after it. The item consists of a deep-fried potato with a fried chicken cutlet, mac and cheese, bacon hot honey jam, scallions and 215 sauce.

Eagles: Broad Street Beast

Now available at Lincoln Financial Field is an 18-inch chalupa shell that includes wagyu beef shank, fried jalapeno poppers, tomatillo avocado salsa, Oaxaca queso, shallots and cilantro.

Cincinnati Bengals: Who Dey Sausage

The Bengals' "Who Dey" chant is the namesake for a 24-inch BBQ cheddar pork sausage served on a bun with pickled red onions, jalapeno and BBQ sauce.

Carolina Panthers: The Big 'Dilla

The two-foot smoked adobo chicken quesadilla includes a cheddar and jack cheese seared tortilla plus cilantro, pico de gallo and chipotle crema.

Denver Broncos: Beast in a Blanket

Denver's take on a two-foot item is a hot dog with brisket burnt ends, cheddar and goat cheese wrapped in a puff pastry. It's topped with secret sauce, avocado cream, pickled onions and jalapeno.

Houston Texans: Battle Red Berry Bird

Houston rocks battle red uniforms, therefore, it's only right that a concession item named after the threads is created. Fried chicken breast is tossed in a strawberry buffalo sauce and topped with coleslaw, pickles and Cajun cheese curds on a challah bun.

stories.headline: Nigeria 'weren't there yet' after FIBA Women's World Cup exit - Rena Wakama
stories.summary: The Nigerian women ended their campaign with a 111-56 loss to France on Monday, their third defeat in as many Group B games after opening with a 99-81 loss to South Korea and then falling 71-67 to Hungary.
stories.body:
Nigeria lasted just three games of the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup, a loss to France in their final group game on Monday sending the African champions crashing out of the tournament.

But coach Rena Wakama says D'Tigress are still rebuilding and "weren't there yet" after a disappointing tournament that ended without a win.

The Nigerian women ended their campaign with a 111-56 loss to France on Monday, their third defeat in as many Group B games after opening with a 99-81 loss to South Korea and then falling 71-67 to Hungary.

While this last defeat to France was somewhat expected, the manner of the loss was sobering for a team that arrived in Berlin two years removed from a historic run to the quarterfinals of the Paris Olympics.

"For us, it's tough because a lot of people saw what we did in 2024, and the reality of where we are today is that we're in a rebuilding process," Wakama said at the post-game press conference.

"I think connectivity is a big thing for myself, my team, my staff. So, where we are today isn't where we were two years ago. And I had to explain that to my team."

France made the gulf between the teams clear almost immediately, racing to a 31-13 lead after the opening quarter and stretching that advantage to 65-26 by halftime.

Nigeria scored 13 points in each of the first three quarters and shot just 28% from the field for the game, while France shot 58%. The French also made a record 22 3-pointers, passing Japan's newly set total of 20 from their defeat of Mali on the opening day. France's Gabby Williams scored 25 points, Janelle Salaun 19 and Marine Johannes 17.

"Huge credit to France," Wakama said. "They are a phenomenal team. A lot of those players are in playoff shape. They play in the WNBA. And my players, we just weren't there yet to be able to compete at the level that they were competing at."

The result completed a sharp reversal from Paris 2024, where Wakama guided Nigeria to victories over Australia and Canada and made D'Tigress the first African basketball team, male or female, to reach an Olympic quarterfinal.

It also represented a step back from Nigeria's last appearance at the Women's World Cup in 2018, when D'Tigress became the first African team to reach the quarterfinals after beating Greece 57-56 in Tenerife.

Nigeria qualified for the 2022 tournament but did not participate after the Nigerian government withdrew the country's national basketball teams from international competition.

This time, there was little momentum from the start.

South Korea opened Nigeria's tournament with a 99-81 victory, with Jihyun Park scoring 27 points. Portland Fire's Amy Okonkwo led D'Tigress with 22 points as Nigeria stayed within three points at halftime before collapsing in the second half and getting outscored 51-36 in the last two quarters.

The opportunity to recover came against Hungary, but Nigeria spent almost the entire game chasing after falling behind 21-13 in the first quarter. Dorka Juhasz finished with 19 points and 16 rebounds as Hungary won 71-67, despite a late Nigerian rally that produced 25 fourth-quarter points.

The overall performance was made even more disappointing because the team had engaged in a whirlwind of preparation that started with training camp in Chicago and games against WNBA teams, to playing three games against China before rounding out their pre-tournament preparations in Europe.

Wakama acknowledged that Nigeria's preparation for the tournament had been good, but said that competing at this level requires more: "We had a great preparation, but I think there's another level that we have to get to in that preparation.

"And huge credit to the NBBF for supporting us and giving us an opportunity to be here, but I know in my mind there is another level we have to get to."

Okonkwo, who had been Nigeria's most productive scorer through the opening two games, was held to just three points against France, missing all eight of her field-goal attempts. She finished with eight rebounds and three assists.

"It was a tough game," Okonkwo said. "France is a great team. We saw it at the 2024 Olympics. We've seen it every qualifier. They are a really great team, and they really came out to play today.

"I think we just struggled to find our rhythm early and we were unable to get the win today or really stop them."

France had also beaten Nigeria 75-54 in the group stage of the Paris Olympics and defeated D'Tigress by a much closer margin of 93-86 when the teams met during the World Cup qualifying tournament in Villeurbanne in March.

Amid the disappointment, Wakama pointed to the silver lining of performances of Nigeria's younger players as one of the positives she will take away from Berlin.

"I'm the most proud of our fight," she said. "When you have a new team, and I have so many young players, I think I have about five or six young players on this team that have never been at this stage before, some that just graduated college.

"Grace Efosa played about 20 minutes. She came on and gave us 15 points. Miriam, these are names you guys will hear in the future. But I threw my young ones in the fire, and they responded for me. So I'm super proud of that."

Grace Efosa-Aguebor's 15 points came in just over 20 minutes and led Nigeria against France. She shot 4 of 7 from the field, including 2 of 4 from 3-point range, and made five of six free throws.

Nigeria leave Berlin 0-3 and bottom of Group B, a result that Wakama believes is as disappointing as it reflects where this version of D'Tigress are compared to what the team accomplished two years ago.

The task now, she says, is finding out what that next version of the team will be: "We can't rely on two years ago's success.

"So who we are today, we're still figuring that out. And I know we will."

stories.headline: Burning questions for all 32 NHL teams this preseason
stories.summary: With training camps opening up around the league, here's the biggest storyline for every club.
stories.body:
It has been nearly three months since the Carolina Hurricanes raised the Stanley Cup for the second time in franchise history. Since then, the 2026 draft brought a new wave of prospects to each team, and there was a whirlwind of activity on both the trade and free agency fronts.

But now, with temperatures getting cooler and many more pumpkin-flavored items hitting the shelves, it's almost time for hockey to return.

To help get you fully prepared for the coming weeks of the preseason -- as teams make final decisions on rosters, lineups and goaltending tandems -- let's take a look at the biggest lingering question for all 32 clubs, thanks to ESPN reporters Ryan S. Clark (Western Conference) and Kristen Shilton (Eastern Conference).

How to watch the 2026-27 NHL season on ESPN networks -- including 100 exclusive games and the out-of-market package (over 1,050 games).

Atlantic Division

Boston Bruins

How will they respond to a roster retool?
The Bruins meant business when they picked up JJ Peterka from the Utah Mammoth in June for a pair of first-round picks. Peterka's numbers last season were average -- 25 goals and 47 points in 82 games -- but he's only 24 and has potential to be a breakout skater for the B's. Or so they hope.

Peterka was the centerpiece of Boston's offseason acquisitions that otherwise notably included the return of Connor Clifton and trade addition of Will Borgen. Meanwhile, Viktor Arvidsson and Andrew Peeke departed in free agency, leaving Boston without a top-five scorer and minute-munching defenseman.

The Bruins will now look inward -- perhaps to James Hagens cracking the roster full time after getting his feet wet with two NHL games last season. But that's still a "what if" -- one of a few for Boston as they head into coach Marco Sturm's second season. General manager Don Sweeney still hasn't locked in a new deal for restricted free agent Matthew Poitras, although there's time left. Poitras spent most of 2025-26 with the AHL's Providence Bruins, but there is space for him at the NHL level if he's ready. How the Bruins put all of their pieces together will be a fascinating scene.

Buffalo Sabres

Does Buffalo need a workhorse goaltender?
It's an open secret the Sabres are trying to trade for Connor Hellebuyck. The three-time Vezina Trophy winner wants out of Winnipeg -- where he remains signed through 2030-31 with an $8.5 million annual cap hit -- and Buffalo could use a dominant presence in the crease.

Buffalo got through the regular season and ended its historic playoff drought last season via a goaltending tandem of Alex Lyon and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen. That duo eventually struggled late in the postseason run as Buffalo blew its shot at an Eastern Conference finals appearance.

Going back and forth between netminders isn't always a viable long-term strategy, and investing in a player of Hellebuyck's caliber ideally makes Buffalo a significant threat in the Atlantic again this season. At 33, Hellebuyck has the experience and impressive résumé to elevate Buffalo's most glaring area of need. The issue -- beyond Winnipeg appearing in no hurry to honor Hellebuyck's trade request -- is that while he earned individual hardware (including a Hart Trophy in 2025) and a gold medal at the 2026 Olympics, his NHL postseason record (24-34) has left something to be desired. Is that a reflection on him, or the Jets? We won't know until Hellebuyck suits up somewhere else.

Will Buffalo give in to Winnipeg's demands to make a preseason splash? And if the Sabres can't land Hellebuyck -- what will they do to ensure goaltending doesn't halt their progress again?

Detroit Red Wings

How will the new GM right the ship?
This is a two-parter for the Red Wings. It starts with who is going to replace Steve Yzerman as the team's general manager? Yzerman stepped down in July, and the search for a replacement has been mostly quiet since then (other than Detroit Tigers assistant GM Jeff Greenberg pointedly removing himself from the candidate conversation).

What hasn't been so silent is the reverberations around captain Dylan Larkin's ongoing standoff with the team following his June trade request. The club is under no obligation to let Larkin go to one of his few desired landing spots -- the 30-year-old is under contract through 2030-31 with an $8.7 million AAV -- and even if the Red Wings wanted to play ball, any return has to reflect Larkin's status as one of Detroit's top skaters (with 67 points in 74 games last season).

It's a lot of drama for the incoming GM to tackle right away. If Larkin stays, how does that affect team chemistry? Does he retain the captaincy? The still-unnamed GM should have an easier time with another internal issue though -- getting RFA Simon Edvinsson's next deal done so he's ready to be in the lineup. Whomever fills Yzerman's shoes will just have to show their mettle in a hurry.

Florida Panthers

Will a facelift help them bounce back?
It was strange to see the Panthers outside the playoff mix last season -- but perhaps it was inevitable they'd slide down the standings following multiple championship runs (and minus captain Aleksander Barkov for the season).

But this isn't the same team it was in 2025-26. The Panthers broke the internet -- again -- trading for Brady Tkachuk to enhance a top-six forward group headlined by his brother, Matthew Tkachuk. The bottom half of Florida's lineup looks different as well, with Mackie Samoskevich, Evan Rodrigues and Jesper Boqvist gone in free agency and veterans Lars Eller and Garnet Hathaway added.

Another critical transition for Florida is in the crease now that long-time starter Sergei Bobrovsky signed as a free agent in Toronto and has been replaced by the often-inconsistent Jacob Markstrom (working with a new backup too in Akira Schmid). GM Bill Zito has never shied away from shaking things up. Has he pushed the right buttons here again?

Montreal Canadiens

Are the young stars ready to take the next step?
The Canadiens are fresh off an Eastern Conference finals appearance, and though Montreal ultimately fell against the eventual Stanley Cup champions, there was a litany of positives to mull over in the offseason.

The team leaned on its rising stars to perform last spring, and what will propel Montreal forward this fall is the development of those same players.

All eyes will be on Jakub Dobes to stand out as Montreal's definitive No. 1 starter -- he inked a three-year contract extension in June (with an AAV of $5.357 million) that reflects how he backstopped the Canadiens' incredible run.
Forward Ivan Demidov also got paid this summer, with an eight-year, $73.2 million deal that put Montreal's full faith behind the 20-year-old to build off a rookie campaign in which he led all first-year players in scoring (with 62 points in 82 games).
Juraj Slafkovsky's growth -- and superb postseason production -- is also exciting for Montreal to monitor, as his line with Cole Caufield and Nick Suzuki was a difference-maker.

The Canadiens have chosen to run it back. GM Kent Hughes didn't target outside help to address a potential need at second-line center or infuse the bottom six with some pop. Montreal is betting on its collection of burgeoning young stars to be a top contender in the East again.

Ottawa Senators

Is Ottawa ready to break out after saying goodbye to Tkachuk?
A change can do you good ... or so the song goes. The Senators brokered a deal with Florida in June to honor Brady Tkachuk's trade request. It was a tough break on multiple fronts; Tkachuk is a consistent point-per-game producer and carried leadership responsibilities within the group, so there is a notable gap to fill.

Getting William Eklund from San Jose one day after the Tkachuk deal gave Ottawa an immediate option next to Tim Stutzle on Ottawa's top line, while infusing some renewed hope into their entire offensive operation. Andre Burakovsky was also brought in and carries with him championship-caliber experience to benefit the Senators on and off the ice. And with Tkachuk gone, there could be fresh opportunities for incumbents such as Drake Batherson and Dylan Cozens.

The best-case scenario is that the Senators shift into a different gear up front in the wake of their former captain's departure. Couple that with Linus Ullmark picking up where he left off in a personally excellent postseason and the Senators could be more than one-and-done in the playoffs again.

It's time for Ottawa to embrace being maybe not a better team without Tkachuk, but a different one -- maybe with a chip on its shoulder. There's enough talent left to make it happen. Can the Senators make the mindset shift to embrace a new version of themselves?

Tampa Bay Lightning

Do they have the right mix on defense?
The Lightning certainly have superstar Nikita Kucherov's future to contend with as the franchise's top player approaches free agency in July, and a decision sooner than later would alleviate some anxiety. Beyond an extension for Kucherov, the team will need to figure out how to get beyond the first round, after four consecutive early playoff exits.

That all starts with how the Lightning fare defensively going into this season. Darren Raddysh is gone; John Carlson is in. And what about captain Victor Hedman? The veteran had a tough season between injuries and taking leave to handle personal matters. The 35-year-old hasn't suited up since March 19, and ended 2025-26 with only 17 points in 33 appearances. It was Raddysh -- since jettisoned in a sign-and-trade with Toronto -- who was the driver in offensive production from the blue line, with 70 points in 73 games.

Carlson should help replace some of what was lost with Raddysh -- he tallied 14 goals and 60 points in 71 games -- and is generally reliable. But Tampa Bay truly needs Hedman to be back on his game. That's when the Lightning excel. Hedman is an integral player at 5-on-5 and both special teams. How the Lightning reset defensively will answer early doubts about whether they have what it takes to make noise in the East again.

Toronto Maple Leafs

What does Sergei Bobrovsky have left to offer?
Incoming GM John Chayka wasted absolutely no time remaking the Maple Leafs. Since May, Chayka has turned Toronto inside out: he replaced coach Craig Berube with Jim Hiller, got Darren Raddysh on an eight-year deal via sign-and-trade with Tampa Bay, selected Gavin McKenna No. 1 in the 2026 draft and signed veteran Sergei Bobrovsky as the Leafs' answer to its previous goaltending woes.

That last move could be what defines the season ahead for Toronto -- good or bad. Bobrovsky -- reunited with his former Panthers' teammate Anthony Stolarz as the Leafs' projected tandem -- has won two Stanley Cups. He has won the Vezina Trophy twice. But Bobrovsky is coming off an abysmal season in which often cringeworthy play added up to the first sub-.900 save percentage of his career since 2011-12. What's more, he will be 38 when the season begins.

"Gamble" might be an understatement describing Chayka's move in pushing the Leafs' chips in on Bobrovsky with a three-year, $21 million deal. Because Chayka also traded Joseph Woll, and Stolarz struggled last season compared to a strong showing in 2024-25. The Leafs finished last in the Atlantic a year ago, so Chayka had to effect some change to account for that disappointment. Backing Bobrovsky, and how that decision pans out, will be telling of his early success getting back in control of an NHL team.

Metropolitan Division

Carolina Hurricanes

Are special teams the key to unlocking another Cup run?
One of the Hurricanes' great consistencies over the past decade has been an exceptional penalty kill -- until suddenly it wasn't. That was the case last season when Carolina dipped to 11th in the league short-handed (at 80.5%) and likely only finished that high because Jaccob Slavin, a penalty-killing dynamo who was limited to just 39 regular-season contests due to a lower-body issue -- bumped the Hurricanes up when he returned late in the season.

Carolina should have Slavin healthy from the jump for 2026-27, and that's a serious win when it comes to leveling back up short-handed. And if the Hurricanes can complement an elite penalty kill again with a top-10 power play -- which they found last year thanks to a surge from December onward that carried over into the postseason -- then they'll be among the top Cup favorites again.

Will that come to pass? Slavin is integral, but so is goaltending, particularly when the team is down a man. Carolina is relying on its less-experienced duo of Brandon Bussi and Pyotr Kochetkov in net after letting veteran Frederik Andersen walk in free agency. It would be a pity for the Hurricanes to have goaltending be a detriment toward reaching their full potential.

Columbus Blue Jackets

Will stability end their postseason drought?
The Blue Jackets missed out on the playoffs for the sixth straight season, and coach Rich Bowness claimed it was because Columbus' players were unbothered by losing. Ouch. Bowness vowed to change the team's culture, and to send a message that would see the Blue Jackets back into playoff contention.

Columbus has already dealt with offseason distractions. First it was Zach Werenski's reported desire to be traded that has since been walked back and dismissed by him and the club. Then it was Kirill Marchenko -- an impending RFA next summer -- apparently refusing to sign an extension and putting the 70-point skater's future with Columbus up in the air.

Does keeping Marchenko and Werenski both happy long term depend on what Columbus does this season? If so, that's a mountain of pressure to place on Bowness right down through the lineup, which is still lacking in secondary scoring talent usually found on playoff rosters. The early schedule could be a bonding moment for Columbus -- or reveal fractures too deep to bandage over. Just how shaky is their foundation?

New Jersey Devils

What is the prognosis offensively?
It's fair to ask whether Jake Allen, 36, is steady enough to handle being the Devils' No. 1 goaltender this season. But how Allen fares -- and how much heavy lifting he has to do -- will depend on what New Jersey can put together in front of him.

New GM Sunny Mehta traded a conditional first-round pick and a second-rounder for Luke Evangelista. It was a surprising move that gives the Devils another option to be duking it out for top-nine minutes. Mehta landed Evan Rodrigues and Jesper Boqvist from Florida in exchange for former starting goalie Jacob Markstrom, and the Devils signed Anthony Mantha in the offseason, too. Where do they all fit with the Devils' established skaters?

And speaking of that, the other perennial concern for New Jersey's offense is whether it will consistently include a healthy Jack Hughes. The team's star forward has an unfortunate history of unavailability. Maybe that's why Mehta was willing to (over)pay on insurance and create some real competition for jobs this season. Will his strategy pay off with four chemistry-filled lines for coach Sheldon Keefe to roll every game?

New York Islanders

How well will they respond to a full season of Pete DeBoer?
GM Mathieu Darche raised eyebrows when he fired coach Patrick Roy and brought in Pete DeBoer as replacement in the final weeks of the season. Why not just let Roy run out of the clock on 2025-26?

Well, it gave DeBoer a lay of the Islanders' landscape before spending several months ruminating on a retool. Now we'll see what DeBoer has up his sleeve to get New York back in the playoffs -- and if it's a plan his team can get behind.

Let's start there for the Islanders. Ilya Sorokin needs to be a brick wall if the Isles intend to make up for consistent scoring struggles. What Sorokin requires to put up Vezina-worthy numbers is a defense keeping pucks off him, and elevating the blue line is where DeBoer's impact can be felt immediately. Matthew Schaefer is exceptional, but won't carry the back end alone -- he could even be testing a new role for the left-shot heavy Islanders by transitioning to his off-side. Is that DeBoer's best option though? Adam Pelech and Ryan Pulock have been a strong pairing, and keeping them as one seems wise, plus there's depth with Tony DeAngelo and Alexander Romanov.

How DeBoer molds the Islanders' defense will directly affect how well Sorokin can support a team that, outside of Mathew Barzal and Bo Horvat, is lacking in top-end skill. Sorokin has almost single-handedly gotten New York to the playoffs in the past. DeBoer is here now to help make that feat a full-team effort.

New York Rangers

Are they actually better off after this offseason's transactions?
It's not that GM Chris Drury hasn't tried. He didn't go get Pavel Dorofeyev from Vegas and sign him to a seven-year, $77 million contract so that the Rangers could languish as an Eastern Conference bottom-feeder. Once again, it's more that Drury has New York set to rely on its top-six forward group to win the day without giving the team enough secondary support throughout the lineup.

The Rangers have options -- Oliver Bjorkstrand, Joe Veleno and Eeli Tolvanen were added to the equation there along with Will Cuylle, Joe Veleno and others -- but is there too much pressure on New York to sink or swim with its top six? And will that be even tougher to do even with Dorofeyev in the mix but given Vincent Trochek no longer is?

New York must offer Igor Shesterkin some goal support if they expect him to keep putting up top-tier numbers. Bringing on Marcus Pettersson adds some hope the Rangers can do that. There's been enough drama for the Blueshirts the past two seasons; the focus must now be on consistency, with contributions across the board. It will quickly become clear if Drury did enough to offer coach Mike Sullivan the ability to execute on such a vision.

Philadelphia Flyers

How do they line up down the middle?
The Flyers certainly went for it when they put in a five-year, $90 million offer sheet for Ducks center Leo Carlsson. Their bold play didn't work -- the Ducks matched the terms to retain Carlsson -- but Philadelphia taking a chance there was a not-so-subtle nod to their need for a top-line upgrade. Does going after Carlsson -- and failing to get him -- have a residual effect on the Flyers' remaining incumbent centers who will be battling in preseason for the opportunity to secure that top slot?

As it stands, Philadelphia has Trevor Zegras (coming off a career-best 67-point season), Noah Cates, Christian Dvorak and Sean Couturier as options for their pivot slots. There's also the outside chance for Jett Luchanko. A first-round pick in 2024, he is one of the organization's top prospects, and he has been marinating long enough and needs to join the NHL ranks. Is this the time when he can take advantage of opportunity with a strong training camp and boost Philadelphia's overall prospects right now at center?

Competition is never a bad thing. The Carlsson business might not reflect the Flyers' full faith in who they have, but it's on the group there now to show they can help Philadelphia be sound enough down the middle to keep pace in the competitive Metro.

Pittsburgh Penguins

What is this team's identity for 2026-27?
The Penguins are in an intriguing spot. They made a surprising playoff appearance last season and could be in position to push for that outcome again in 2026-27 -- if enough things go their way.

Evgeni Malkin's production at age 40 in potentially the final campaign of his career is one factor. Whether Arturs Silovs can be a true No. 1 goalie -- while getting enough support from backup Sergei Murashov -- is another. GM Kyle Dubas added around the edges in the offseason with Nicholas Robertson, Andrei Kuzmenko and Trevor van Riemsdyk coming on board, and Rutger McGroarty should be recovered from an injury he dealt with over the summer.

These are all positives. But just how good can Pittsburgh realistically be? And more than that -- how good do they want to be? Are the Penguins delaying an inevitable rebuild? Or is having Malkin and Sidney Crosby around reason enough to keep their ambitions high no matter the cost?

Dubas was active enough to suggest Pittsburgh is going to come out of the gate intending to compete for a postseason berth again. How long that remains their ultimate driver will depend on those X factors: Malkin, Silovs and overall team defense.

Washington Capitals

How do all of the new faces fit in?
The Capitals didn't make the playoffs last season and GM Chris Patrick appeared to take that personally. Because he went all-in on boosting Washington's offense by acquiring Jordan Kyrou via trade with St. Louis, adding big-ticket free agent winger Alex Tuch, and solidifying overall depth with signings like Boone Jenner and Vincent Desharnais.

Oh, and Alex Ovechkin is back too -- which might be the best news of all given how he's continued to elude Father Time.

It's a lot of cooks in the kitchen, and that can be either a good problem to have for coach Spencer Carbery or an obstacle toward finding the right combinations. Washington saw firsthand last season what can happen when a key forward -- in that case Pierre-Luc Dubois -- suffers an early-season injury, and playoff hopes suddenly slip away without comparable talents to backfill. The Capitals wanted to guard against that by giving the team more options going into this season.

But what does the final picture look like if everyone stays healthy? Is Washington doomed to endure some growing pains in pursuit of the perfect lineup? Or does chemistry spark immediately and make Carbery's job all the easier? If nothing else, Patrick is putting money where his mouth is offering the Capitals every shot at a quick turnaround.

Central Division

Chicago Blackhawks

How much of an impact will Bowen Byram have in his first season in Chicago?
No one defenseman can mask every issue on the back end that's plaguing a team. Yet there is a belief that Byram should be able to provide improvement in a few areas. Especially when the Blackhawks have already invested quite a bit. Chicago traded away a first-round pick before signing Byram to a contract earning $12.5 million annually.

Although that extension starts next season, this season will provide quite a bit of insight into what the future could look like for the Blackhawks. Chicago was one of the most porous defensive units in the NHL in terms of allowing high-danger scoring chances, scoring chances and shots. That's just one area where Byram could have an impact. Another is on the offensive end in which the Blackhawks' points leader among defensemen last season was Louis Crevier with 25 points, whereas Byram finished with 42 points in 82 games for the Sabres last season.

Colorado Avalanche

What must happen for them to win the Stanley Cup?
Continuity is crucial for any team challenging for a Stanley Cup. The Avalanche have that, with 17 returning players that were on the roster that advanced to the Western Conference finals last season. That includes Cale Makar, who just signed a record-setting contract extension, and will be the NHL's first $20 million AAV player when it kicks in.

But what was learned from being swept by the Golden Knights that could make the difference? Avs general manager and team president Joe Sakic found ways to adjust in certain areas. He moved on from some familiar figures in the lineup such as Ross Colton and Valeri Nichushkin, while also making alterations he believes can have an impact on the lineup. Sakic signed a veteran Stanley Cup-winning winger in Jaden Schwartz and was able to add some younger players such as Zachary L'Heureux and Fedor Svechkov to give them more depth.

Dallas Stars

Do they have enough depth to challenge for a Stanley Cup?
Advancing to three straight Western Conference finals only to then get eliminated in the first round in 2026 leads to a number of questions. There are concerns around how the defensive structure failed to find consistency against the Wild. Dallas allowed the second fewest goals per game in the regular season at 2.71 per contest -- only to have an opening round that saw them allow more than four goals per game in three of its four losses to Minnesota.

There are also questions about how the Stars struggled to receive production throughout their lineup. Six players scored all 15 of the first-round goals the Stars recorded, with nine belonging to Wyatt Johnston and Jason Robertson. It's a jarring contrast for a team that had nine players reach double figures during the regular season.

Minnesota Wild

What ends up happening with Quinn Hughes by the time the season is over?
Wild GM Bill Guerin told SKOR Radio North that he was "confident" that the club could sign Hughes to a new contract.

But it goes back to something else Guerin said too, which is that the Wild could not force Hughes to sign anything.

Hughes' future was a talking point from the moment he arrived last December in a blockbuster trade. His arrival saw the Wild go from a playoff team to one that could be ready to challenge the Western Conference's power dynamic.

That only amplified during the Winter Olympics and the playoffs, when his performance won the United States its first gold in men's hockey since 1980, and got the Wild to the second round. Hughes' place as one of the best defensemen in the league can't be questioned. But as for where he will be playing come this time next season? That is the question.

Hughes addressed his situation at the NHL/NHLPA player media tour. He said the contract "is going to be done whenever I feel like it needs to be done. I don't feel backed up against a wall." Hughes added that he wanted to take his time and make a decision that "is going to be good for everyone."

Nashville Predators

Exactly where do they fit within the Western Conference?
As one of three teams that fell short of a playoff spot by four points last season, the Predators could potentially challenge for a playoff berth in 2026-27. Of course, the same could be said for the other two Western Conference teams in their position. That only adds to the belief that the Western Conference has a chance to be more competitive this season than it was last season.

Nashville still possesses its veteran core from last season, and added some new yet experienced players that first-year GM and team president Chris MacFarland knows from his time as GM of the Avs. Could those tweaks make a difference?

St. Louis Blues

What path will the Blues' young core guide the franchise on this season?
The Blues missed the playoffs by four points last season, which paved the way for one of the league's more aggressive offseasons.

They traded away Jordan Kyrou, while adding Brandon Carlo, Mason McTavish and Connor McMichael, the latter of whom came over from the Capitals in the Kyrou trade. McTavish and McMichael add to a group that could see the Blues have nine players younger than 25 make their opening night roster.

Those additions -- along with the potential growth from Dalibor Dvorsky and Jimmy Snuggerud in their sophomore campaigns -- could dictate what road the Blues take this season, especially if it means improving upon a return that saw them finish with the ninth-fewest goals per game in 2025-26.

Utah Mammoth

Will the Mammoth disrupt the power structure in the Western Conference?
Every Western Conference finals series since 2020 (aside from the COVID-impacted 2021 playoffs) has featured the same four teams in some combination: The Avalanche, Golden Knights, Oilers and Stars. It was that way again last season, with the Avs and Golden Knights.

Vegas didn't sail smoothly to that spot, as the Mammoth took a 2-1 first-round series lead before the Golden Knights won consecutive double-overtime games en route to eventually reaching the Stanley Cup Final. Playing such a tight series against the Golden Knights presented the possibility the Mammoth could be ready for more.

How does an offseason that saw them make big swings -- trading away JJ Peterka while adding proven veterans Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck -- impact their rise?

Winnipeg Jets

Can the Jets plot the right course to reach their desired destination?
Connor Hellebuyck issued a statement through his agent saying that he has requested a trade, and this is the primary issue facing the Jets right now. The keyword there being "primary," because there are other items for the Jets to be concerned about:

The depth that helped them capture the Presidents' Trophy in the 2024-25 season struggled for consistency in a 2025-26 campaign that saw them miss the playoffs for the second time since 2017-18.
Kyle Connor, Mark Scheifele and Gabriel Vilardi accounted for 46% of their goals.
The Jets were in the bottom 10 in goals per game overall, underlining the need for them to receive additional scoring help.

It's an even more pressing concern when they finished eight points out of a playoff spot, and 10 points above finishing last in the Central.

Pacific Division

Anaheim Ducks

Do they have enough to make a significant defensive improvement?
The Ducks finished last season in the bottom five of high-danger chances and scoring chances allowed, which raised its own set of questions. Losing their veteran defensive trio of John Carlson, Radko Gudas and Jacob Trouba in the offseason only enhanced that discussion. Plus, their goaltending also had its challenges, with the Ducks having the fourth-lowest team save percentage in 5-on-5 play.

Anaheim navigated all of that to reach the playoffs for the first time since 2018, with the intent of returning to the postseason in 2026 knowing that six of its seven defensemen on the current roster are younger than 25. It's a group that's anchored by Jackson LaCombe and Pavel Mintyukov, and is expected to see Drew Helleson, Tyson Hinds, Tristan Luneau and Ian Moore carve out a larger role for a team trying to build off last season's achievements.

Calgary Flames

How will they foster the next wave of their youth movement?
One way to conceptualize development is to think of it like phases. Matt Coronato, Dustin Wolf and Connor Zary were part of the first phase in the Flames' rebuild. Now it appears the Flames are about to embark on a second phase, attaining a firmer grasp on what they have with Matvei Gridin, Samuel Honzek, Simon Nemec and Zayne Parekh.

Gridin, Honzek and Parekh were all first-round picks drafted by the Flames who had extended runs with the team in 2025-26. Gridin and Parekh each appeared in 37 games while Honzek had 18, with the belief that the 2026-27 campaign could see them become more established.

Nemec was drafted second overall in 2022, and came over in an offseason trade with the Devils. The 22-year-old, who signed a five-year extension shortly after he was traded, is also looking to reinforce why he could be a key figure in their long-term plans.

Edmonton Oilers

Can Mike Babcock succeed where others didn't and win a Stanley Cup?
There are plenty of questions that can be asked when it comes to the Oilers. But at the same time... why even ask those questions when it all comes back to the narrative about the need for the Oilers to win it all with superstar center Connor McDavid entering the first of a two-year contract extension?

Babcock arrives facing the type of questions that are usually reserved for a new coach, along with controversial ones that aren't reserved for most coaches who've been behind an NHL bench. Babcock resigned as coach of the Blues Jackets during the 2023 preseason among questions of his conduct. The NHL investigated the situation this summer and ultimately cleared him to be hired by Edmonton.

Still, the Oilers only have one real question to consider: Is this the year they win it all?

Los Angeles Kings

Did they do enough this offseason to ensure they'll score more goals?
No team entered the playoffs last season averaging fewer goals per game than the Kings. Then again, there were only three teams in the NHL overall that averaged fewer goals per game than Los Reyes.

Those struggles were further reinforced when they were swept in the first round, tying for fewest goals per game in the postseason at 1.25.

Kings GM Ken Holland used the offseason to hire Peter Laviolette with the notion his system can lead to more goals. Holland also added more help up front by signing Erik Haula and Mats Zuccarello, and bringing back Corey Perry in free agency after he was moved at the trade deadline. Will that lead to more offense?

San Jose Sharks

Is this the year the rebuild officially ends and the Sharks make the playoffs?
Every rebuild has a pattern. Even rebuilds that fail have patterns. Yet the ones that are declared to be successful reach a stage in which they breakthrough in a way that creates the narrative they could be ready for more.

All of that is exemplified by the Sharks in 2025-26, who had a 34-point improvement that set them up to finish four points out of the final Western Conference wild-card spot. That's the sort of outcome that presents the idea that the playoffs could be within reach this season.

So were the moves they made in free agency, adding more proven veterans around a young core led by Macklin Celebrini and Will Smith that's seeking to guide Los Tiburones to the playoffs for the first time since 2018-19.

Seattle Kraken

How much can this season shape the Kraken in the years to come?
Could this be one of the more interesting pivot points in the Kraken's brief existence? They made advantageous attempts to lure Artemi Panarin and Jason Robertson to Seattle via trade last season, only to come up short. While the team missed on those two, they remain a potentially attractive destination due to more than $17 million in cap space (per PuckPedia), and one of the NHL's strongest farm systems.

That also comes with the caveat that any hypothetical move comes in a season in which decisions must be made with Vince Dunn, Ryker Evans, Jared McCann and Shane Wright, among others. Dunn and McCann are slated to hit free agency, while Evans and Wright will be restricted free agents next summer.

Vancouver Canucks

What can Canucks expect from their centers this season?
One of the items facing Manny Malhotra in his first year behind the Canucks bench is figuring out what he can get out of a center group featuring Elias Pettersson, Marco Rossi and Filip Chytil.

Pettersson led the Canucks with 51 points last season, yet the goal for Malhotra and his staff is to help him recover to being the consistent offensive threat that made him a franchise cornerstone when he signed his long-term contract (his current deal pays him $11.6 million annually through 2031-32).

Rossi, who arrived in the Quinn Hughes trade, had his season disrupted by injuries. When healthy, he was averaging 0.70 points per game. As for Chytil, he's also seen his career disrupted by injuries, and sustained another one in February that caused him to miss the rest of the season. If he can stay healthy, there's a chance he could provide the Canucks with another top-nine option down the middle.

Vegas Golden Knights

How will they define success in Ryan Craig's first season?
First-time NHL coaches are typically provided some sort of grace period, because all parties understand there is something of an adjustment. Yet the situation facing Craig ahead of his first season is quite different compared to most new coaches.

Craig isn't in charge of a team with a young roster that's trying to develop. He's taking over a Golden Knights team that's one of the best in the NHL, and was two wins away from capturing the Stanley Cup three months ago. The Golden Knights are no strangers to having a new coach -- they've now made two coaching changes in less than a year -- and fully understand what it means to quickly establish continuity.

All of this comes with the context that those previous coaches also had experience running an NHL bench. Craig has been on an NHL bench before. He was hired as a Golden Knights assistant back in 2017, and was in that role for six seasons before he was named the head coach of their AHL affiliate. Out of anyone, he surely understands the high expectations for this franchise.

stories.headline: Detroit Pistons offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: Will Detroit return to the top of the East? Looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season.
stories.body:
How will the Detroit Pistons follow a season that ended in a playoff thud?

Detroit rolled to a 60-22 record and clinched the East's No. 1 seed, then stumbled out of their first-round series against the Orlando Magic and ultimately fell in the second round. Restricted free agent Jalen Duren has received scrutiny for his playoff performance, especially pertinent as his camp and the Pistons are still far apart in contract talks.

The Pistons made some other moves, too, but none that brought them a second star to cast next to Cade Cunningham. Will it be enough to flip their postseason script? ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Let's dive into the Pistons, who remain in contract purgatory with Duren.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Pistons coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: John Collins, Isaiah Joe, Taurean Prince, Gary Harris

Key subtractions: Tobias Harris, Isaiah Stewart

Key retentions: None

The Pistons' offseason is still in limbo as negotiations with restricted free agent Jalen Duren have stalled. Detroit believes its sent Duren a fair offer considering the totality of his 2025-26 season -- including his underwhelming playoff showing -- while Duren feels like he's checked off all the boxes to get more. Losing Harris and Stewart will be a big test to their culture -- or a signal they have to win a different way than in the last two seasons. They added shooting on the margins with Joe, Prince and Harris. And assuming Duren's deal gets done before camp, Ausar Thompson's contract is next on the docket. -- Vincent Goodwill

Zach Kram's offseason grade: C-

All-NBA center Duren seems likely to return in restricted free agency, but Detroit traded away Stewart -- its longest-tenured player -- and effectively exchanged Tobias Harris and Caris LeVert for John Collins and Isaiah Joe, respectively. That seems like a moderate downgrade, all things considered, and the Pistons didn't acquire significant scoring and playmaking help for Cade Cunningham.

Despite coming off a 60-win season, they'll need further internal improvements from Duren and Ausar Thompson to pose a greater playoff threat next spring. -- Kram

What we learned this offseason
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: Cunningham's life didn't get much easier.

The Pistons can't claim much progress this summer: They're still at loggerheads with restricted free agent Duren, they replaced Harris with Collins, and they added Joe to address their wonky spacing.

While guard Ebuka Okorie represented good value at the No. 17 pick, his up-and-down summer league play suggested he's unlikely to be a difference-maker as a rookie. After shocking the world by winning 60 games, the Pistons opted not to make a splash.

Cunningham has endured much more challenging circumstances as Detroit's franchise player, but he is poised to enter next season without a quality secondary creator once again. That roster hole didn't stop the Pistons from claiming the East's top seed last season, but it certainly reared its ugly head in the playoffs. Opposing defenses found success by loading up on Cunningham to short-circuit Detroit's offense, especially late in games.

The Pistons' top eight players all logged at least 1,700 minutes or appeared in at least 72 games last season, raising the possibility of regression if they can't maintain that standard of availability. Detroit should be able to count on another season of elite defense, but it must keep searching for a dynamic sidekick to improve its playoff outlook. -- Golliver

The big question: Is Detroit already at a disadvantage in the East by not pairing Cade Cunningham with a second star?
Not exactly. It's fair to wonder if this offseason looks underwhelming considering a 60-win season and a second-round loss to No. 4 seed Cleveland Cavaliers in Game 7. The front office clearly wanted a co-star for Cunningham but nothing materialized. However, president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon has been prudent in his tenure, and the Pistons could be the team with the greatest incentive to make an in-season move, especially with the top of the East getting stronger. Their cap situation is still favorable, even with the uncertainty with Duren. -- Goodwill

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 8
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Pistons' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

How did the Pistons go from worst to first in the East from 2024 to 2026? They improved by about 17 net points per game in that time, with about six of that being improvement by Cunningham, Duren and Thompson. Another six was moving out some of the bad players, like Jaden Ivey, James Wiseman and Killian Hayes. The rest was adding better players like Paul Reed, Duncan Robinson, and Harris (who left this offseason). -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Biggest X factor this season
F John Collins

Detroit made some meaningful changes to its rotation over the summer, none bigger than Collins' replacing Harris. Collins isn't on Harris' level as a one-on-one scorer or team defender, but he has advantages because of his youth, athleticism and sneakily excellent jump shot (40% on 3s over the last two seasons).

Collins hasn't reached the playoffs in three seasons, so he'll need to transfer his skill improvements to a winning situation. But it's possible that he could add a newly dynamic element to a Pistons team in need of it. -- Kram

Betting insight from our experts
Fantasy insight ahead of the season: The Pistons brought in 28-year-old Collins this offseason to replace 34-year-old Harris as the starting power forward.

Collins is bigger, more explosive and more of a finisher than Harris at this point in their respective careers. Collins showed in his days with the Hawks that he operates well as a finisher next to a dominant offense-creating point guard, setting single-season-bests of 21.6 PPG and 10.1 RPG next to Trae Young. This season, Collins will be playing off MVP-candidate Cunningham, and could be a late-round fantasy sleeper with the potential to produce one of his best seasons. -- Andre Snellings

stories.headline: 2026 Ballon d'Or: Full men's, women's short lists, host city change, more
stories.summary: The 2026 Ballon d'Or short lists are out. Here's who could win the biggest individual prizes in men's and women's soccer.
stories.body:
It's nearly that time again.

The 2026 Ballon d'Or awards -- the annual ceremony in which France Football Magazine crowns the best men's and women's players in the world -- are fast approaching, with the short list for each award announced on Tuesday.

The Ballon d'Or trophies are handed out based on the criteria of: "1) Individual performances, decisive and impressive character, 2) Team performances and achievements, 3) Class and fair play."

Any player in world football is eligible, no matter the league they play in or their country of origin, and the short lists are decided by a jury of 100 journalists from around the world. So who is nominated for this year's awards, and who could win?

When is the 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony, and why isn't it in Paris?

The 2026 Ballon d'Or awards, which have long been presented by France Football Magazine, will be handed out on Oct. 26. There will be a difference this year, though: The star-studded ceremony will not take place in Paris. Instead, it will be held in London at The London Palladium theater to mark the gala's 70th anniversary.

The first Ballon d'Or ceremony was a much more humble affair, held in Blackpool, England, and awarded to 41-year-old star forward Stanley Matthews.

Matthews was an all-time England great who spent the majority of his career at Blackpool and Stoke City and, when announcing the venue change, was described by organizers as a "true ambassador of football."

"As the Ballon d'Or becomes of septuagenarian age, it is fitting in such a landmark year to celebrate the finest present-day exponents of the beautiful game in the beating heart of the country that first conceived of it," organizers added.

Full 30-player Ballon d'Or short list

Jude Bellingham
Club: Real Madrid

Country: England

Bellingham didn't win a trophy with Real Madrid for the second year running, but the all-action midfielder was an important pillar of England's bronze medal-winning display at the 2026 World Cup. The 23-year-old scored seven goals at the tournament and his virtuoso two-goal display against Mexico in the round of 16 is likely to go down in Three Lions' folklore.

Pau Cubarsí
Club: Barcelona

Country: Spain

A debut nomination for 19-year-old center back Cubarsi, who played an important role in Barcelona's 2025-26 title win before being crowned Best Young Player at the World Cup after playing every single minute of Spain's monumental victory, keeping seven clean sheets along the way. He is also nominated for the Kopa Trophy, which is awarded to the best player aged 21 or younger.

Marc Cucurella
Club: Chelsea / Real Madrid

Country: Spain

Cucurella was a mainstay for Chelsea in the Premier League in 2025-26 before completing a transfer to Real Madrid during the World Cup. The energetic left back played every single minute for Spain at the tournament, and even provided two assists before ending his summer as a world champion.

Ousmane Dembélé
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: France

Dembélé won the 2025 Ballon d'Or after starring for Paris Saint-Germain in the first of their back-to-back Champions League wins in 2024-25. Having repeated the feat with the club last season, the 29-year-old winger also accrued six goals and two assists for France at the 2026 World Cup.

Luis Díaz
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: Colombia

Diaz was part of a Bayern Munich team that amassed 122 league goals in just 34 Bundesliga matches last season, with the Colombia forward accounting for 15 of them. He then scored one goal and notched an assist as his country were jettisoned from the World Cup at the round-of-16 stage on penalties by Switzerland.

Bruno Fernandes
Club: Manchester United

Country: Portugal

One of the most reliable creative forces in the Premier League, Fernandes scored nine goals and weighed in with 21 assists for Manchester United in 2025-26, thus breaking the league's single-season assist record in the process. It then came as little surprise to see the Portuguese maestro crowned Premier League Player of the Season.

Erling Haaland
Club: Manchester City

Country: Norway

Despite suffering an extended fallow period during the second half of the 2025-26 Premier League campaign that saw him notch just three league goals between January and mid-April, Haaland still powered to a third Golden Boot with 27 goals in 35 games. The Norway striker then scored seven goals in his debut World Cup outing while becoming one of the most popular personalities at the tournament.

Gabriel Magalhães
Club: Arsenal

Country: Brazil

Gabriel kept 17 clean sheets for Arsenal in their title-winning 2025-26 season, helping to solidify one of the most effective defensive lines in world football.

Harry Kane
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: England

One of the favorites to lift the 2026 Ballon d'Or, Kane scored an astounding 67 goals in 58 games for Bayern Munich last season across all competitions, including 36 goals in 31 Bundesliga games. However, the prolific striker did fall short in his quest to win both the Champions League and the World Cup -- though he did technically captain England to a third-place finish at the latter.

Achraf Hakimi
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Morocco

Hakimi made only 18 appearances for PSG in the league last season but still ended up as a title and Champions League winner with the French giants. The right back also won the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations with Morocco -- although they lost the final to Senegal, the result was overturned by organizers due to their opponents prematurely leaving the pitch -- and he reached the quarterfinals of the World Cup the following summer.

Lamine Yamal
Club: Barcelona

Country: Spain

Yamal scored 24 goals in 45 games for Barcelona in all competitions as the Catalans wrapped up the Spanish league title in 2025-26. A lingering hamstring injury forced the winger to sit out the very start of the World Cup as he managed his fitness, but he was able to feature in the group stage in a reduced capacity. He then gradually grew in stature as the tournament progressed, with Spain ultimately emerging victorious.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Georgia

Instrumental for Paris Saint-Germain in their second successive Champions League victory, the Georgia winger relished playing on the big European stage and registered a sequence of 10 goals and six assists along the way.

Marquinhos
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Brazil

Rock-solid at the heart of the Paris Saint-Germain defense, 32-year-old center back Marquinhos split his 32 appearances equally between Ligue 1 and the Champions League in 2025-26, and ended up winning both.

Sadio Mané
Club: Al Nassr

Country: Senegal

A fifth career nomination for veteran forward Mane, who pitched in with 14 goals in 36 games for Al Nassr last season as they were crowned champions of the Saudi Pro League. The 34-year-old Senegal star also guided his side to the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations.

Lautaro Martínez
Club: Inter Milan

Country: Argentina

Martinez won the Serie A and Coppa Italia double with Inter Milan in 2025-26, finishing as top goal scorer in the former and being crowned the best striker in the league as a result. He also scored three goals in eight games to help Argentina reach the final of the 2026 World Cup.

Kylian Mbappé
Club: Real Madrid

Country: France

He may have gone two seasons without winning anything with Real Madrid, but Mbappe hasn't been shy in putting himself forward for the 2026 Ballon d'Or, remarking that this year would be a "good year" for him to win it. The striker scored 42 goals in 44 games for Madrid and duly carried his fine form into the World Cup with France, where he claimed the Golden Boot with an impressive 10 goals to his name.

Nuno Mendes
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Portugal

A league and European double winner with Paris Saint-Germain with the Portugal international routinely proving to be among the very best left backs in the world.

Lionel Messi
Club: Inter Miami

Country: Argentina

With a record-extending 17th Ballon d'Or nomination, Messi is once again in the running to claim what would be a ninth career Ballon d'Or at the grand age of 39. The superstar is still scoring and assisting freely with Inter Miami in MLS, but his inspirational performances -- encompassing eight goals and four assists in eight games -- for Argentina at the World Cup this summer saw him come close to captaining his country to a second successive World Cup triumph, only for the dream to fall apart against Spain in the final.

Michael Olise
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: France

Nominated last year but finishing 30th out of 30 in the polling, Olise has seen his stock rise immeasurably over the past 12 months. The stylish, skillful attacking midfielder was an intrinsic part of the Bayern Munich side that cantered to the 2025-26 Bundesliga title and while he may not have found the net for France during their run to the World Cup semifinals this summer, Olise did lay on seven assists -- three more than any other player.

João Neves
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Portugal

He may only be 21 years old, but Neves has already developed into one of the most coveted midfielders in world football. A metronomic presence in the middle for Paris Saint-Germain and a Ligue 1 and Champions League double winner last time out.

Willian Pacho
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Ecuador

Highly rated Ecuador center back Pacho made 44 appearances for Paris Saint-Germain last season, winning the league and European double.

Julián Quiñones
Club: Al Qadsiah

Country: Mexico

Quiñones outscored Ivan Toney and Cristiano Ronaldo in the Saudi Pro League with his club Al Qadsiah, bagging 33 goals to top the chart in 2025-26 before scoring four goals for Mexico at the 2026 World Cup.

Declan Rice
Club: Arsenal

Country: England

One of the most dependable and versatile midfielders in world football, Rice was a Premier League title winner with Arsenal in 2025-26, with five goals and 11 assists thrown in for good measure. He also started all seven of England's games at the World Cup, even scoring in the topsy-turvy bronze medal tie against France.

Rodri
Club: Manchester City / Barcelona

Country: Spain

The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner endured a fairly underwhelming 2025-26 season at club level with Manchester City though he did seem to recapture his form just in time for the World Cup, where he pulled the strings in magisterial fashion for Spain on their way to lifting the trophy before wrapping up a £65million transfer to Barcelona in the aftermath.

Fabián Ruiz
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Spain

After an incredible season with Paris Saint-Germain and Spain, Ruiz can now claim to have won it all by adding a World Cup winners' medal to an enviable collection that already included the European Championship, the UEFA Nations League, the Champions League, various league titles and a host of other major honors.

Ferran Torres
Club: Barcelona / Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Spain

Torres scored 21 goals in 49 games for Barcelona in their title-winning 2025-26 campaign, though his crowning glory must surely be scoring the goal that saw Spain pip Argentina to win the 2026 World Cup. He left Barcelona this summer to join PSG.

William Saliba
Club: Arsenal

Country: France

Alongside defensive partner Gabriel, Saliba formed a watertight barrier at the back as Arsenal cut and thrust their way to the 2025-26 Premier League title.

Dayot Upamecano
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: France

Upamecano won the 2025-26 German title with Bayern Munich and was named in the Bundesliga team of the year thereafter, despite only making 24 appearances. He then played eight times for France at the 2026 World Cup, conceding just two goals before Spain knocked them out at the semifinal stage.

Vinícius Júnior
Club: Real Madrid

Country: Brazil

Vinicius Junior scored 22 goals in 53 games for Real Madrid last season, but frustratingly ended the campaign with little to show for his attacking endeavors. He then contributed four goals and an assist for Brazil at the World Cup.

Vitinha
Club: Paris Saint-Germain

Country: Portugal

Another of Paris Saint-Germain's double winners, Vitinha made 50 appearances and scored seven goals for the French giants over the course of the 2025-26 season while being named in both the official Ligue 1 and Champions League teams of the season.

Full 30-player Ballon d'Or Féminin short list

Selma Bacha
Club: OL Lyonnes

Country: France

As one of the leading left backs in the game, Bacha helped Lyonnes to a domestic treble and another Champions League final, adding 13 assists to help maintain OL Lyonnes' dominance.

Barbra Banda
Club: Orlando Pride

Country: Zambia

With 14 goals in 21 games, Banda has not slowed down her ruthlessness in front of goal, making her one of the most prominent attackers in the world.

Klara Bühl
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: Germany

Even though she registered 10 goals for Bayern Munich this season, it is her 23 assists across 37 matches that have made Bühl a worthy nominee, leading the German champions to a domestic treble.

Esmee Brugts
Club: Barcelona

Country: Netherlands

In her first nomination for the Ballon d'Or, Brugts registered 13 goals and 11 assists across 48 matches for Barcelona highly contributing to another quadruple-winning campaign.

Mariona Caldentey
Club: Arsenal

Country: Spain

Caldentey helped guide Arsenal to the inaugural Champions Cup title and retained Spain's Nations League trophy with her meticulous work rate and control in the midfield.

Scarlett Camberos
Club: Club América

Country: Mexico

As the first female Mexican player to be nominated for the Ballon d'Or, Camberos has already made history. She scored 27 goals and registered seven assists when leading Club América to win the Concacaf Women's Champions Cup.

Kerstin Casparij
Club: Manchester City

Country: Netherlands

The Dutch defender started almost all of City's victorious Women's Super League campaign, captaining the side when needed, adding seven assists and helping the team to another FA Cup victory.

Temwa Chawinga
Club: Kansas City Current

Country: Malawi

Chawinga's impressive 15-goal tally played a key role in leading the Kansas City Current to the NWSL Shield, highlighting her crucial contribution to the team's outstanding regular-season campaign.

Cata Coll
Club: Barcelona

Country: Spain

Keeping 23 clean sheets in total, Coll ensured Barcelona claimed another quadruple and even kept a clean sheet during the Champions League final. She only conceded 18 goals all season in 39 games.

Melchie Dumornay
Club: OL Lyonnes

Country: Haiti

Leading Lyonnes' attack, Dumornay netted 21 goals in the 2025-26 season, winning Première Ligue Player of the Year and guiding Lyonnes to another Champions League final. She added 12 assists to set up her teammates, making her one of the most valuable players in the game.

Caroline Graham Hansen
Club: Barcelona

Country: Norway

With 17 goals and 16 assists in 45 games, Graham Hansen was as prominent as ever during Barcelona's quadruple-winning season.

Alex Greenwood
Club: Manchester City

Country: England

The England defender captained Manchester City to domestic a domestic double, ending Chelsea's supremacy over the Women's Super League as well as securing another FA Cup title in a comprehensive 4-0 win over Brighton at Wembley.

Patri Guijarro
Club: Barcelona

Country: Spain

Guijarro played a vital role in Barcelona's engine room, ensuring the juggernauts stayed on top. Amid injuries and changes, the Spain midfielder's skill did not waver, making her one of the best players in the world.

Pernille Harder
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: Denmark

A prolific scorer, Harder's 35 goals and 12 assists made sure Bayern's domestic treble dreams stayed intact. She has won a domestic title every year since 2016 despite playing for three clubs in three different countries; 2025-26 was no different.

Yui Hasegawa
Club: Manchester City

Country: Japan

As one of the most underrated players, Hasegawa has flown under the radar, yet the Japan international started 20 WSL matches for City last season and maintained the English champions' standard to claim a second domestic title. She won her 100th cap for Japan during the country's title-winning Women's Asia Cup run.

Rose Lavelle
Club: Gotham FC

Country: United States

Lavelle was a crucial figure in securing Gotham's NWSL Challenge Cup with 14 goals and five assists in 40 games.

Mapi León
Club: Barcelona / London City Lionesses

Country: Spain

León was one of Barcelona's longest-serving players and started in 10 of the club's 11 Women's Champions League games on their way to lifting the trophy for the fourth time. This summer, though, she moved to emerging WSL team London City Lionesses.

Lorena
Club: Kansas City Current

Country: Brazil

The first-choice goalkeeper for both Kansas City Current and Brazil, she is of the most established goalkeepers in South American women's soccer. She is also nominated for the Women's Goalkeeper of the Year award.

Melvine Malard
Club: Manchester United / Chelsea

Country: France

Malard was one of Manchester United's standout players as they reached the Women's Champions League quarterfinals in what was the club's debut in the competition, notching four goals and four assists over the course of eight appearances. This summer, she made a blockbuster move to Chelsea.

Manaka Matsukubo
Club: North Carolina Courage / Chelsea

Country: Japan

Named the NWSL's best midfielder in 2025, Matsukubo followed up with a superb start to the 2026 season with five goals and four assists in nine games before joining Chelsea in July. At international level, she won the Women's Asia Cup with Japan.

Vivianne Miedema
Club: Manchester City

Country: Netherlands

Manchester City ended their decade-long wait for the Women's Super League title, and they could scarcely have done it without Miedema. The skillful forward started all but three of their league games last season, scoring 10 goals.

Ewa Pajor
Club: Barcelona

Country: Poland

When Barcelona need goals, Pajor is the first name they call upon. She was the 2025-26 Women's Champions League top scorer with 11 goals in 10 appearances. She is among the favorites for the Ballon d'Or Féminin.

Clàudia Pina
Club: Barcelona

Country: Spain

As prolific as her teammate Pajor is, Pina strikes a close second. She scored 21 goals in 27 games in Liga F last season, ending as the competition's top scorer.

Alexia Putellas
Club: Barcelona / London City Lionesses

Country: Spain

A favorite to win her third Ballon d'Or Féminin award, Putellas returned to being Barcelona's most crucial player in another landmark year, captaining the club to yet another quadruple. However, this summer, she ended her 12-year stay at the Camp Nou to join the London City Lionesses.

Wendie Renard
Club: OL Lyonnes

Country: France

Even at 36 years old, Renard is still among the gold standard of center backs in the game. She was one win away from extending her record of eight Women's Champions League titles, only to see defeat to Barcelona in the final.

Alessia Russo
Club: Arsenal

Country: England

With 18 goal contributions in 22 WSL games last season, Russo remains one of the best attacking threats in world soccer. She is also just one of two England players to make the short list alongside Manchester City's Alex Greenwood.

Khadija "Bunny" Shaw
Club: Manchester City

Country: Jamaica

With Manchester City not in European football last season, Shaw got to work focusing on scoring in the WSL and did so superbly. She finished as the competition's top scorer with 21 goals.

Momoko Tanikawa
Club: Bayern Munich

Country: Japan

Still only 21 years old, Tanikawa was an influential presence in the Bayern Munich midfield that helped the club reach the Women's Champions League semifinals, only to succumb to a hard-fought defeat to eventual champions Barcelona. At international level, she won the Women's Asia Cup with Japan.

Caroline Weir
Club: Real Madrid / OL Lyonnes

Country: Scotland

Last year, Weir became the first Scottish player to be nominated for the Ballon d'Or Féminin, and she follows up with another short list this time out. She netted 14 goals for Real Madrid in Liga F last season, as well as appearing in the Women's Champions League. In June, she moved to OL Lyonnes.

Tessa Wullaert
Club: Inter Milan

In her second season in Italy, Wullaert excelled with Inter Milan, scoring a league-high 14 goals, albeit the club did not manage to beat AS Roma to the Women's Serie A title.
